speechtext: I would like to ask the Minister of Militia whether or not he proposes to permit any of t'he soldiers at present in training in the camps in Nova Scotia to engage in farm work for the spring season. I have received some requests from the people of my county who are desirous of having their boys home for a couple of weeks and who wish to ascertain if leave will be granted if they make application. Last year permission was given. In Nova Scotia the farm work has hardly 'begun yet, and the desire is expressed that the boys might be given leave to assist in it.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
subtopic: EMPLOYMENT OF ENLISTED MEN ON FARMS.
speechtext: This year the conditions in reference to giving leave to members of the Canadian Expeditionary force to engage in farm work are entirely different from those of a year ago. Last year we had a great many soldiers in the country; this year there are not many left, and most of them have been warned to prepare to embark for overseas. We have had a few requests similar to that to which my hon. friend refers, hut owing to existing conditions we have not been able to see our way clear to grant permission. The time when our soldiers are expected to embark for overseas is not very far distant, and there will be very little time for them to go on the farms. In addition, the granting of leave for such work tends to demoralize the force, and also a great deal of difficulty has been experienced because of men contracting contagious diseases, such as mumps, measles, and so on. For all these reasons we have not been able to grant leave to our soldiers, and in that respect we have laid down one rule to apply throughout the Dominion. Many of the troops at Aldershot will be going overseas shortly.

speechtext: On the motion of Sir Thomas White (Minister of Finance) for the second reading of'the resolutions reported from Committee of Ways and Means.

Mr. Speaker, before the resolutions are read the second time, in pursuance of notice given some days ago, I desire to -move an amendment, but before doing so, I wish to make a statement of my reasons for moving my amendment. In presuming to discuss the Budget proposals laid before the House by the Minister of Finance, I consider the outstanding fact is that the revenues dur-

heavy to be borne. In looking over the Labour Gazette, published by the Department of Labour, I find estimates of the cost of the weekly food supply for a family of five at different times. The estimate has increased from $6.95 in 1910, to $10.45 in
1917-in round numbers an increase from $7 to $10.50, that is $3.50, or fifty per cent. If there are a million and a half of families in the Dominion of Canada, this increase would mean that besides the $60,000,000 of additional taxation that the Government is levying upon the Dominion of Canada, the people are bearing an additional burden of $275,000,000 in the increased cost of living as compared with 1910.

Is that money going
out of the country?
No.

How then can the
people be bearing an additional burden?

Because they are, that is
all.
It is only changed from one shoulder to the other.

They have to pay the
money. The people who are getting the money are not complaining, but the people who are paying it, and there are more people paying it than getting it. For instance, the Davies Packing Company have $2,800,000 worth of food products in their storage, and the people who buy it have to pay for it. But the Davies people are not complaining.
I understood the hon. gentleman to speak of the people as a whole.

I am speaking of the
people in the large majority. The statement of the Minister of Finance on increased taxation, and the statement of the Department'of Labour on the high cost of living, indicate that the people of Canada are paying approximately $330,000,000 a year more than they were paying in 1910.
I do not consider it remarkable, under these circumstances, that there is not a satisfactory development of the basic industries of the Dominion. I call the attention of the Minister of Finance to these facts with a view to suggesting to him that, instead of heaping up taxation without regard to its incidence, it is certainly for him to study the condition^ and adjust the burden of taxation so that it shall be in accord with the ability of the people to bear it.
Naturally, Mr. Speaker, being from Western Canada, the conditions as applied to that

part of the country appeal to me more directly than the conditions in other parts. May I be pardoned if I occupy a few minutes of the time of the House in dealing with the conditions there particularly? Whatever may be said of the great natural resources of Canada, its mines, its timber, its fisheries, or whatever else may be counted, it is admitted now that the great resource of Canada upon which the development and the greatness of Canada as it is to be must necessarily depend, is to be found in the Prairie West. In the thousand miles of fertility lying between the Red River and the Rocky Mountains, and in the development of that fertility and bringing it into a state of productiveness, will Canada find her greatness. So, it is a matter of deep interest to every citizen of Canada, wherever he may live, to know whether development is progressing in that part of the country or not and if it is not, why, and what can or may be done to improve or increase that development. The facts, shortly, are that in the Prairie West, in 1910, according to the Census and Statistics Monthly, there were practically 13,000,000 acres of land under cultivation. Inl911there were 16,500,000 acres of land under cultivation, an increase of 3,500,000 acres as compared with 1910. In the year 1912 there were 18,318,000 acres under cultivation, an increase of 1,750,000 acres over 1911, and in 1913 the area under cultivation was 18,398,000 acres, an increase of less than 100,000 acres over the previous year. In 1916 the area under cultivation was 19,910,000 or an increase of 1,500,000 acres over 1912, a period of four years. We have an increase of
3.500.000	from 1910 to 1911, an increase of
1.750.000	acres from 1911 to 1912, and an increase of 1,500,000 from 1912 to 1916. To use a favourite expression of.the Minister of Finance, the slackened development in the Northwest synchronizes with the application of his financial policy to the affairs of this country. I am bound to conclude that there is a most intimate connection between the two circumstances.
If I may be permitted to deal with a feature of this development that is not directly connected with the tariff but which is, I submit, most intimately connected with the Budget, that is to say with the development and revenues of the country,
I would like to mention this fact. We have heard a great deal about the price of wheat that prevails at the present time and it is largely understood that the farmers of the Prairie West are practically holding up the rest of the Dominion and the British

Empire in the matter of foodstuffs, particularly wheat. The Prairie farmer is supposed to receive $3 a bushel and the price of flour in the Maritime provinces is, I think, $15 a barrel as a result. The suggestion is that the Maritime province man is paying $3 a bushel to the Prairie farmers. As a matter of fact, the wheat crop of last year, except a few million bushels, left the farmers' hands at a maximum price, so I am credibly informed, of about $1.75 per bushel. That w.as the utmost he got and it ran down from that to possibly $1.30 or $1.20 - a good price, a price that was satisfactory to the farmer at the time, and he is certainly not complaining about it. Because of that price he is doing everything he can to extend his farming operations. The price of $3 a bushel for wheat is the price that fixes the cost of a barrel of flour in the Maritime Provinces and the farmers did not get the difference between the $1.75 and the $3. That w,as the result of market manipulation. As a result of market manipulation on the officially estimated amount of 70,000,000 bushels of wheat of last year's crop in dealers' hands, not in farmers' hands, and acquired by the dealers at a maximum of $1.75 a bushel, somebody pays a bonus to somebody of $70,000,000 and over, and the Maritime Province man who has to pay $15 a barrel for his flour is helping to pay that ' $70,000,000.
Are the consumers in the Maritime Provinces paying more for a barrel of flour than they are paying for a barrel of flour in any other country in the world?

I could not tell my hon. friend anything about that; I can only tell him that the farmer got $1.75 for his wheat, that the man who bought it was selling it at $3 and over, and that it was the selling price of wheat that fixed the price of flour.
Will the hon. gentleman tell the House the amount of grain in the hands of farmers on the first of May, when the $3 price obtained?
No, I cannot, nor can anybody else.
I notice that hon. gentlemen from the We3t are 'always clamouring for cars to move out the grain and claiming that the farmers in the West have not been able to get .their grain out.

Nobody can tell how much grain there was in the farmers' hands at that time. There may' have been much or little, but we know what was in the
dealers' hands and we know how much that grain appreciated in value. And we know that that appreciation is what fixes the price of flour, and that the farmer does not get it. If I am within the rules I wish to carry this matter a little further, and perhaps my remarks may be slightly aside from the Budget discussion; but when $70,000,000 are in question and when the people of Canada are paying their share of that $70,000,000, they are entitled in this House of Commons to any information that they can get on the subject., It is an abnormal condition, it is a tremendous addition to the burdens carried by the people of the country, and they are entitled to know something about how it occurs that such burdens aTe being carried. To follow the suggestion of my hon. friend from Peterborough (Mr. Burnham), if the farmer got the $3 and the Maritime man paid the price for this flour, the money would be in the country just the same; but when the farmer does not get it and the Maritime man pays the price for the flour, then the farmers, at any rate, are interested in knowing who gets it and how it happens.

Is it not a fact that
on analysis of the statistics of the United States Congressional Board that was appointed for investigating these very things, also of the Minnesota Board and the New York Board, and of the Fruit Associations of Georgia, Alabama, Tennessee, ' Florida, California and Oregon, also of the Wheat Boards of Kansas and the Northwest, it has been ascertained that the farmer, allowing for the steadiest possible conduct of the trade in agricultural products, receives only from 57 per cent to 61 per cent of the final price of the grain after it has been manufactured?

I wish to assure you, Mr. Speaker, that on the conclusion of my . argument it will be found that I am absolutely speaking to the point; though it may seem that in laying the foundation of my remarks I am somewhat aside from the
4 p.m. question. It is obvious that, if the consumers of Canada are paying an abnormal price for the first necessity of life, and the producers of that necessity of life in Canada are not receiving that price, an undue advantage is taken of the consumer on the one hand and of the producer on the other, and that the burden militates against the ability of both producer and consumer to carry on the ordinary affairs of life. The question of grain prices in western Canada depends largely upon transportation' and manipulation, and when the exigencies of transportation can be turned to account by those whose business is manipulation, as they are systematically turned to account, then all the people of this country, both producers and consumers, suffer, and the well-being and the welfare of the country, and the revenues of the country, suffer correspondingly. Last fall, in the province of Alberta, served by three competing railroad lines, there was a grain embargo for a considerable period on all these lines, the Canadian Pacific, the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Northern. Those who are familiar with the conditions will know'that when a railroad is unable or unwilling to transport the farmers' grain to the market, the result is a depreciation in the price of his grain. That must be obvious. And I am saying here in my place in Parliament and on my responsibility as a member, that in the earlier part of the last market season, 1916, those three railroad companies refused to haul grain from points in Northern Alberta. I am not saying anything about the rest of the country, I am speaking of what I know.	And because they refused to haul that grain, the price of grain to the farmer was seriously depreciated. From time to time during the market season the newspapers have , noted that one railroad company or the other, and frequently the three, had placed an embargo upon the transportation of grain to Fort William or to Minneapolis.
[Mr. Oliver.7	v
They were willing to take the grain of Alberta to the storage elevators in Calgary or Moosejaw or Saskatoon, but they had placed an embargo upon the transportation of grain to Fort William or Minneapolis.
I wish to draw the attention of the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Railways, and the Government of this country to the fact that, so far as I know, last season was the first season in the Dominion of Canada, or in the British Empire, when railways simply set the common carriers law of Britain at defiance, to the detriment of the farmers of the West in the price that they received for their produce. In the season of 1915 there was a very large production, and it was not possible for the railroad companies to carry that grain forward as it would be desired. They therefore placed embargoes, so-called, upon the carriage of grain. But these embargoes were of necessity. The embargo, of last year, on the other hand, was not an embargo of necessity; it was an embargo of defiance of the rights of the people of Canada, a defiance with the authorization, I believe the active authorization, and knowledge of this Government. By no other means could it have been. effected, We	have in
Canada three transcontinental railroads- -that is, if the Government has not already tom up the rails of one or two of them. The Transcontinenal Railway was built for the sole purpose of providing an all-year-round market for the grain of the western farmer by giving him an all-rail haul to an open ocean port all the year round. The grain there, would not be held back in interior elevators under the control of professional manipulators, thus depressing the price to the farmer and making possible an increase of the price to the consumer. The interior storage elevators at Moosejaw, Calgary and Saskatoon were used last winter for the express and sole purpose of enabling the manipulation of grain prices.

Those who manipulated
the grain prices were able tp hold quantities of grain in the interior elevators, thus keeping down the price to the farmer, while holding the grain against the eastern buyer.
I repeat that that was the only purpose that these elevators were used for last winter. There was no shortage of railing stock for the carrying forward of that grain as it should have been carried forward. No condition warranted the refusal of the railroad

Why did the Grain
Growers' Company not help them out?

The farmers of the West expect the Government to exercise in their behalf the authority which they possess. I am drawing the attention of the Government to these facts, and the Government, I am sorry to say, does not seem to be very sympathetic or receptive.
Are not the farmers of the West entitled to store their grain in these interior elevators?
They are, if they want to.
Would that not be exactly the same thing as storing it in Port Arthur? I do not see any difference. They did not have to sell.

If 1 want to ship my grain to Fort William I have a right to ship it there. When the railway company says to me: we have put an embargo on the shipment of grain Ito Fort William; we will take your grain to Saskatoon, but not to Fort William-I say that that is trespassing upon my rights. Further, that trespass is committed in somebody else's interest; it would be nonsense to argue anything else.
I have been referring to the enormous burden laid upon the people by reason of the appreciation of $70,000,000 in the price of grain. This increase was made possible because of the holding back of the grain. There was no reason why the grain should not have gone forward, because ample facilities existed for that purpose. This country has put hundreds of millions of dollars into the construction of railroads for the purpose of facilitating the transportation of grain. One of these railroads has for years been under the absolute and direct control of the Government. Held back, (therefore, in the interior elevators or at Fort William, this grain was made the subject of manipulation against the interests of the farmers-and somebody gets $70,000,000 to which he is

not entitled. Certainly tlie farmer dees not get it. If the crop of Ithe prairie West were carried forward from day to day to the Atlantic seaboard, as it can and should he carried forward, such stupendous manipulation of prices as took place last year and as has taken place in other years would not be possible? All that the farmer has asked is that he get the Liverpool price. Under present conditions the man in Liverpool ought to get his wheat at the price at which the Canadian farmer sells it, plus carrying costs and charges. When we permit a condition under which $70,000,000 is taken from the consumers, whether in Canada or in England, we are certainly not properly appreciating our responsibilities. The railroads have been built for the purpose of carrying the grain, but we refuse to use them for thai purpose. When such abuses as this occur it is desirable that the country should know who is responsible.
If we find a lack of development, or a failure to develop, we must put the responsibility where it belongs; we must let it be known that it is because the money that was paid for that wheat did not go to the producers of the wheat to enable them to expand production, to increase development, and to increase the ordinary and regular revenues of this country, so that instead of having stagnation we would, to that extent, have development amongst our own peoples, or our Allies and friends in England would get their grain at a lower price.
The question of railway transportation is of enormous importance; it is as important as the tariff question; but the tariff question is the one that is most intimately associated with the resolutions before the House, and I desire to move an amendment to those resolutions having relation to tariff matters, believing that the time has come when it must be apparent to every man, no matter on what side of the House he sits, or what particular faith he professes, that we are in this country pursuing a fiscal policy that is absolutely to the detriment of the country, and that is liable to lead to the financial ruin of the country when the present abnormal conditions give place to those of ordinary life. We shall find ourselves then with the tax-paying power that we had before the war of $120,000,000 to meet interest charges on a total debt of $1,000,000,000. That is an impossible situation, and there must be some other recourse; we must devise some other means of increasing our development in order that we may increase our revenue, and we are not

increasing our development under the fiscal policy that the Minister of Finance has imposed upon this country in the past five years. I believe we cannot expect to increase our development under that policy and the time has come to change that policy, to give our policy another direction that will lighten the burden of taxation upon our people and that will increase our opportunities for the development of the country, as the only means whereby we shall ever be able to carry the enormous burdens that are being laid upon us.
I will say just another word in regard to this matter. Having in view the enormous obligations that we must necessarily take upon ourselves in connection with the war, I must point out that the Government have not taken cognizance as they should of that fact in cutting down the ordinary expenses of the country. What is the answer when the Government is criticised for expenditure? Why, they say: We are spending only a little more or a little less than we did last year; we are spending only a little more than v;e did a few years ago. When this country is going behind at the rate of half a billion dollars per year for war purposes, is it a time to make comparison with what we did in time of peace? Is it not a time to enter upon a policy of economy in regard to ordinary expenditures such as was never thought of in time of peace? This Government do not seem to know that a war is on or that war conditions have to be met. So long as they can borrow money, they are satisfied to spend in any way that is convenient to them. The expenditure of Canada was about $120,000,000 in 1911, when there was no war, and when the country was enjoying a very high measure of prosperity. In this past year we have spent, if I understood the minister correctly, in the neighbourhood of $150,000,000 on current and capital expenditure exclusive of pensions, interest on war debt, and war expenditures, that is, we have spent nearly $30,000,000 more on ordinary accounts than we spent in the year 1911. When we spend more in a year when we are facing a war debt of over $1,000,000,000 than we spent in a year when we were enjoying the highest prosperity and when a war was absolutely unthought of, I submit that under those circumstances the Government are chargeable with absolute neglect of duty and lack of recognition of the terrible circumstances in which the country finds itself. While I urge upon them a policy of economy in the matter of ex-

penditure, I desire to place before the House certain suggestions in regard to a change of tariff policy that, may and I hope, will meet the support of our friends on the other side. I desire to move, seconded by Mr. Carvell:
That all the words after the word "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor :
"In ;he opinion of this House it would be in the rublic interest if the Customs Tariff Act wen- so amended as to provide:
1.	That wheat, wheat flour, and all other products of wheat be placed upon the free list.
2.	That farm implements and *machinery'! farm tractors, mining, flour and saw-mill machinery, and repairs for same, rough and partly dressed lumber, illuminating, lubricating and fuel oils, cement and fertilizers be added to the free list.
3.	That staple foods and food products (other than wheat flour), domestic animals and foods therefor, be admitted into Canada free of duty when coming from and being the product of, any country admitting like Canadian articles into such country free of duty.
4.	That substantial reductions be made in the general tariff on all articles imported into Canada, excepting luxuries.
5.	That the British Preference be increased
to fifty per cent of the general tariff."	'
In regard to the different items of this amendment, may I speak in regard to item No. 1? I am speaking for myself as a representative from the West, and in regard to item No. 1, the position that I would desire to see the House take is this: In the Prairie West we are producing the great basic food products of the world. We are producers of that product for export, as well as for home consumption. In eastern Canada there is no great production of wheat, but it is in eastern Canada where the bulk of our population is situated, where there is the greatest amount of industrial employment, and where the cost of food, and particularly of flour, the basic article of food, is the most important matter in the economy of the worker's family. Those who think with me are prepared to see that basic product admitted into Canada free of duty without regard to the action of any other country; that is to say, in order that our fellow citizens in eastern Canada may have bread as cheap as we can give it to them, we are willing to produce the wheat irrespective of the duties imposed against it by any other country.
Does the hon. gentleman think that the free importation of wheat would greatly lower the price of western wheat?
I dio not know whether it would or not; I am not arguing that. I am merely stating the position we take.

It takes salt and water
and elbow grease, and a lot of other things top. One thing at a time. My hon. friend and I are moving this particular item of the resolution on the principle that as this is our basic product, as it is the basic necessity of our fellow-citizens in eastern Canada. We desire to show good faith in our demands for a lower tariff by asking that this article be placed absolutely on the free list without regard to the duties levied upon it by any other country. Having taken that position, we then ask our friends of eastern Canada to consider this; that in producing wheat in competition with the whole world, which is our position, we must use machinery in very large degree, that without machinery we could not produce the wheat in quantity or at a price, that our wheat fields are situated in .the heart of the continent, that our haul to the sea-board is longer than that of any other export wheat producing area in. the world, that we have that handicap to overcome. We must have machinery in order to produce in quantity, because unless we produce in quantity we cannot produce at a competing price. So we ask our friend in the east to go so far with us as to give us these articles of basic necessity in the production of wheat free of duty, and as cheaply as they can give them to us.

Item No. 3 reads:
That staple foods and food products (other than wheat flour), domestic animals and foods therefor, he admitted into Canada free of duty when coming- from and being the product of any country admitting like Canadian articles into such-country free of duty.
That is a simple statement of trade for trade. We believe that the principle is sound when applied to the basic necessities of life. We believe that both east and west in Canada stand to benefit by that -proposal, and that no part of Canada stands to lose.
Ws ask that substantial reductions be made in the general tariff on all articles imported into Canada excepting luxuries. We are asking the minister to reverse his policy. His policy has been to pile taxes upon taxes, to put tariff increase upon tariff increases, <tto hamper tra^te and increase the burdens jof the people. We have shown him that under his policy there has not been that development of our basic industry which the country needs and we ask him to change his policy, not because this is our policy, but because it is in the interests of Canada that there shall be a change in policy.
Finally we ask that the British preference be increased to 50 per cent of the general tariff. It may 'be suggested that the British preference is a jug-handled arrangement-* that we give, but we get nothing. I maintain that we do get, and we get for everything we give. I read just to-day that a careful calculation of the effect of the British preference upon our imports shows that it has lightened the burden of taxation upon the Canadian people by over $5,000,000 in 1910, by over $8,000,000 in 1913, and I think by nearly $8,000,000 in 1914. I submit that any feature of our tariff that lightens the burdens on our people to-that extent is an advantage to us. The British preference is not something that we are only giving; it is something that we are taking for ourselves, and I maintain that an increase of that preference to 50 per cent would be a still further benefit to ourselves. And if it should be a benefit in anj degree to the people or the industries of the "United Kingdom, are we here to object to that? When we get our share of the benefit, surely we are willing that they should have theirs.

I have not occupied the time of the House in this debate up to the present time, but I wish to go on record in favour of the ideas advanced by the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), not because they are ideas that are favoured very strongly in western Canada so much as because I believe they are of national advantage. We must remember that we are here representing all parts of Canada. I do not want any legislation to be passed in this Parliament that would be of injury to Canada as a whole. At the same time, I want to see the part of the country from which I come given proper attention by this Parliament, and legislation adopted that will be helpful in the development of that section of the Dominion, and advantageous, at the same time, to Canada as a whole. I think I can advance some reasons why the tariff should be reduced, and certain articles placed upon the free list, because-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I regret to be obliged to interrupt the hon. member. If I properly apprehend his remarks, he purposes addressing himself to the subject matter of the amendment of the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver). That amendment I have ruled out of order, and consequently the remarks of the hon. member would not be in order.

I will try and meet your wishes as best I can, Sir. The taxation

proposed by the Minister of Finance in his Budget speech follows lines with which I do not agree. In my opinion we should reach everybody in this country with forms of taxation properly adapted to that end; .at the same time, I believe, that we should relieve the great body of the people from taxation as much as possible. In the West, from which I come, there is a continued demand for relief from some of the burdens of taxation that now exist, and that demand is inspired by a desire to improve the conditions of the farmer of the West and of the western people as a whole. We want to increase production in that country. We want immigration into western Canada to be increased; we want contentment to exist among the farmers of the western prairies. And we believe that the best way to increase immigration, to develop our resources, and to bring about contentment is to relieve the farmers from some of the burdens of taxation that now exist and to adopt other means of raising our revenue. Efforts have been made by the Government to increase production. You cannot increase production by taxing the implements of the farmer. Let me quote an instance from the city of Lethbridge. During the present year about 200 tractors were purchased by farmers in that district, usually through agents in Lethbridge. These machines are to be used for the purpose of increasing production at the call of this Government. In their efforts to increase production the farmers had to pay $60,000 in duties on these two hundred tractors. I say that is unfair to the farmers of western Canada. I have a letter here from a farmer in my own constituency. I do not say I am in favour of all the arguments advanced, but the letter will give some idea of the obstacles the farmer in the West has to face and of the ways in which, according to Ithe opinions of those farmers, there obstacles should be dealt with:-
If the Government is going to set the price of wheat, let them take off the duty on farm machinery and regulate the price of farm labour. Labour is $70 per month and hoard, where we formerly paid $35 for the same thing, and nobody knows what it will be by the day at harvest. Engines are so high we cannot afford to have them. I have a case of ourselves. We want to get an Aultman-Taylor 18-36 engine. It costs in the States $2,400; in Canada, $3,600. Is that right? They claim the duty and freight make up the $1,200 difference. Now, if the Government are going to tell us at what price we shall sell our wheat, let them take off the duty on all our engines and implements and regulate the price of farm labour.
The farmers are paying these exorbitant taxes on productive implements, and at
107 i
the same time they are urged to be loyal and to increase production. I think it is generally the opinion of the people of western Canada, and I know it is the opinion of the organized farmers there, that our system o| taxation should be changed so that we should raise most of our revenue by other methods. They are in favour of an income tax, they are in favour of a land tax and so am I.
I am in favour of an income tax because I believe that is the fairest method of raising the revenue. Under the present system very many men escape taxation who should not be permitted to do so. During the war we are endeavouring to raise money by compelling corporations to pay higher taxation, but we are not getting at people we should get at and those are the wealthy individuals of this country. It has been my experience during patriotic fund campaigns in the southern part of Alberta to find some of the greatest shirkers with regard to patriotic giving to be men of the very greatest wealth. These men are not only shirking patriotic giving but they are not contributing the amount of taxation that they should. The only way they can be reached is by a form of income taxation. In the city of Calgary it was almost impossible to reach one of the wealthiest property owners for the first two years of the patriotic fund campaign or to get a cent from him for any patriotic purpose. That man was not being reached by the taxation of this Government as he should have been reached.
I am in agreement also with the agitation in favour of a land tax. We want the lands that are to-day undeveloped in western Canada developed and we1 can only have them developed by making the speculators who own them release them at a fair price and not hold them for a large advance. We can force them to release that land by imposing a tax on all undeveloped land.
We, from the West, come before this House frequently and advocate certain changes in the form of taxation. As a western representative I want to say that I do not want any taxation to be adopted by this country which is unfair to any other part of the country. In the minds of eastern men, on account of their association day in and day out with the industrial life of the East, there is the idea that the East would suffer if in any way industries were affected by a different form of taxation, or if there were greater freedom of trade, or a reduction in the tariff. But, they should get in touch with the conditions as they
.1683

exist in the West. Many members of this House, members of the Government I know, have visited western Canada in Tecent years but most of their visits have been to the large and populous centres of the West. How many of them have gone out and visited the farmers in their prairie homes? How many of them have come into actual touch with the conditions that the farmers have to face in western Canada? I am afraid that not one member of the Government knows the things that the farmers have to face. If the members of this House got into touch with the conditions that the farmers have to face there they would be more liberal in their views towards the claims that the western farmers are presenting here, through their press and through their organized bodies and more sympathetic with them.
We must adopt some policy that will relieve the burden of taxation upon the farmer especially where the farmer is taxed so heavily on his productive implements. We must do these things to increase production, to add to our immigration and to bring about contentment amongst the people of the West. You know, Mr. Speaker, I am quite sure, that the cheaper the articles of production are, and the cheaper the cost of living may be, the stronger is the appeal to people to come and settle in this country or any other country for that matter. We want to have conditions that will appeal to people to come from other lands and settle in western Canada and help to develop our as yet undeveloped resources. That is one reason, and a very strong reason, for the views which we have been presenting in this House from session to session. I find the sentiment growing in the east in favour of a change in the present method of taxation. I find a newspaper of the standing of the Financial Post calling attention to the fact that there is a great sentiment in favour of the lowering of the tariff and the raising of revenue by other means. I will read just a paragraph from a recent issue of that paper dealing with the Budget recently brought down by the Minister of Finance. The Financial Post says:
On the other hand, the decision in favour of free wheat is an admission of the growing strength of the low tariff element, and that element must be recognized to a greater extent in the future than in the past. ,
That is not frtom the Grain Growers Guide, that is not from a western publication, but it is from a strong financial journal in eastern Canada which supports pro-

tection through and through. It says that the sentiment in favour of a low tariff is growing, it gives as an evidence of the strength of that sentiment the action of the Government in putting into effect free wheat and it says that the Government must pay attention to this particular agitation. Then it goes on to say
This brings the country face to face with direct taxation as a practical solution of raising the heavy revenue which will be required in the future during the period of liquidation of the war debt. This would seem to suggest income tax. Sir Thomas White avoids it, but there is reason to believe that he-or his successor-will in the future employ it.
We must pay attention to the opinion which exists, and which is increasing not only in the Bast but in the West, that we will have to raise revenue by different means from those which we have employed in the past when this war is over. We will have great obligations to meet and we will have to meet .them, but we cannot meet them :by increasing the tariff because if we do we will have an absolutely prohibitive tariff. If we increase the tariff we will discourage production and immigration and Canada will foe in a worse position in the future than it has been in the past. So, we must resort to other means. The present system of taxation as proposed by the Minister of Finance has its good points and it has its bad points, but it will only last for the period of the war. As I understand the position of the Minister of Finance, it is that he objects to bringing into effect an income tax because it will be difficult and costly to operate, but I am of the opinion that if he is in his position as Minister of Finance when the war is over he will have to adopt an income tax and he will have to adopt the principle of direct taxation. That will be necessary and we might as well face the fact at the present time. Let us abandon the policy of increasing the tariff because it is unfair. It is favouritism for the few, and it is a burden for the many. Let us adopt a tax that will compel the people of this country of moderate and large means to contribute their share to the cost of maintaining the Government of the country. It is my view and I believe it will foe the view of this Parliament in a very short time, that we must come to direct taxation in order to meet our obligations. Those of us who have had experience of larger markets in western Canada know that they have been to our advantage. One thing I would like to see provided for by the Fin-

ance Minister is greater accessibility to the markets lying alongside of us. The Government has gone as far as to provide an entry for free wheat into that country, but we want that enlarged because we have found that when we have had an opportunity to enter that market in other cases it has been to the advantage of the western farmers.
It is not my intention to say more on this subject than to emphasize my belief as a western member that the changes in our method of taxation which I have suggested would not be injurious to any other part ,of the country. I want at all times to take that stand; I want to be a member of this House always standing for national.unity. And remember this, that we in the West have been criticised in times past-it even has been insinuated that our people were disloyal, that they were advocating things not in the interest of Canada or in the interests of unity or of our attachment to the Empire. But no part of this country, from the Atlantic to the Pacific has done its duty as have the western provinces since the war commenced. Those who have gone to the front were the very men who were called disloyal in times past because they favoured some methods of taxation that were not considered to the advantage of interests throughout the length and breadth of this country. I say that, knowing what I say. There have been men who have come to this country from other lands, who have left Alberta and gone to the front, men who it was said owed allegiance to other lands rather than to 'Canada; but some of these men left Alberta with every one of the contingents, and some of them have given their lives for the Empire. They are true Canadians. There is just as strong a patriotic spirit in western Canada as in any other part. We have proved it during this war, and we will continue to prove it until the war is finished. I ask this House, I ask the men who represent constituencies east of the Great Lakes, to try and become acquainted with those conditions they will become more liberal in their views toward the demands of the people of western Canada. It is .only by a policy of give and take in this Parliament and this country that we can expect unity to exist between East and West. It is only by a policy of give and take that this can be attained, and I am prepared to favour a policy of that kind in order to have unity, and at the same time to relieve what I believe to be some of the [DOT]burdens of the people of the West.

In order to meet the wishes oi the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), I thought it advisable that the remarks which I purposed making upon the second reading of the resolution should be made upon this amendment, which he now moves on going into Supply. My hon. friend, in the course of his remarks this afternoon, traversed a very wide field indeed. In many ways it was one of the most amazing speeches I have ever heard in this House. There is one thing for which I am really obliged to him, and 5 p.m. that is that he did not accuse the Government in general, and myself in particular, of having been the cause of this war. He certainly attributed to us most of the consequences that have flowed from the war, so far as Canada is concerned. My hon. friend, in the course of 'his remarks, dealt with the situation

existing in the West, and, as I understood him, he seriously suggested that the Board of Railway Commissioners, presided over by Sir Henry Drayton, was in conspiracy with wheat manipulators in Canada, or in Canada and the United States. I think that was the most amazing statement I ever heard in this House. My 'hon. friend did not make it in express terms, hut undoubtedly that was the inference to be deduced from his remarks. I need not say that it is nolt my intention to answer any such argument on the part of my hon. friend from Edmonton; it requires no answer. Knowing the character of the Chairman of the Railway Commission of Canada, who was called upon last winter to meet the most trying conditions of traffic that have ever affected the Dominion, owing to the war and to the movement of munitions and supplies in Eastern Canada, the members of this House will not for one moment credit the statement of the member for Edmonton that the Board of Railway Commissioners were actuated by any other considerations than those of the public interest and the public welfare.
There is another matter to which both my hon. friend from Edmonton and the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) have referred on more than one occasion. My hon. friend from Edmonton referred this afternoon to the fact that we have taken up rails on the Grand Trunk Pacific or National Transcontinental railway, that this Government has torn up the rails of these railways and has had the temerity to send them to France. Well, that is true. But why have we taken such action? We have taken it at the express request of the Imperial Government, who need those rails in order to carry on their operations at the front. I have never been more surprised with regard to any statement made in this House in the course of my experience within its walls, than to hear the leader of the Opposition and the member for Edmonton, by implication, blame this Government for tearing up 100, or 200, or 300 miles of rails on the Grand Trunk Pacific or the Canadian Northern railway to send them forward at the request of the Imperial Government in order that they may be laid behind the lines to bring up munitions needed at the front. I am amazed that any responsible member of this House should blame the Government in any way for the action taken at the express request of the Imperial Government.
