subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext: My hon. friend knows the difficulties of navigation. The fact remains that responsible members of the opposition, including the right hon. leader of the opposition, criticised the Government for taking action asked for by the Imperial Government on account of high imperial necessities.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext: No.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext: Not at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext:
How did the Government proceed? When the request came for rails, the Government did not hesitate for a moment. So far as I am concerned, I would take up half the rails of Canada if they were required at the front. We asked the Chairman of the Railway Commission, a judicial body commanding the implicit confidence of this House and of the Canadian people, to determine from what sections of Canadian railway lines the rails required could be taken. We have acted on their advice, and the rails have gone forward. These rails may be of sufficient importance to determine the issue of

battles, or even the destiny of the Empire. I am not in the slightest degree overemphasizing the importance of steel rails at the front; I defy any man to deny their importance. One thing that has been brought to the attention of this Government and of individual members of the Government who have been at the front is the supreme necessity for steel rails behind the lines, in order to send forward the munitions necessary to win battles under conditions of modem warfare and ultimately to end this war. I hope that we shall hear fewer complaints against the Government for taking the action that we took.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext: Why did you not take rails from the Quebec and Saguenay railway? '

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have the floor. I say, then, that we took this action at the request of the Imperial Government with a view to furnishing means of communication behind the lines. What other position could Ithe Government have taken? Whom should we have asked to advise us as to the railway lines'which could best spare rails?

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext: The Canadian Pacific Railway have a double track along the north shore of Lake Superior which is not in use.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext:
I have no doubt that the Chairman of the Railway -Commission is just .as well aware of the lines along the north shore of Lake Superior as is my hon. friend. I have no doubt that the Commission took the whole position into consideration and that the conclusion they reached was actuated by only one motive, that of taking action with due regard to transportation conditions in Canada and to the high Imperial necessities to which I have referred.
My hon. friend seriously suggested this afternoon that the Government of Canada, or the Board of Railway Commissioners, were engaged in a conspiracy with manipulators in Winnipeg or Chicago for the purpose of preventing the farmers of the West from getting out their grain. Did -any hon. gentleman in this House ever hear such a suggestion as that? He says that the farmers of the West got only $1.75 a bushel for their grain and that somebody got $70,000,000. What impression will the public obtain from that argument of my hon. friend? The impression will be created that the farmer had been paid only $1.75 a bushel for his grain; that somebody had bought that grain at $1.75, held it until the price reached $3 a bushel, and then sold
it all ait a profit of $70,000,000. But my hon. friend overlooks the infinite number of transactions that take place on exchanges, ait Winnipeg, Minneapolis, Chicago. He suggests that by connivance on the part of the Government some individuals have stepped in and taken the difference between $1.75 and $3 a bushel for the grain. I appeal to the common sense of members of the House as to whether my hon. friend had the slightest vestige of reason or logical argument to support the contention which he put forward. The argument has only to be stated to be refuted.
My hon. friend this afternoon made the Government responsible for all the consequences of war. I opened my re-marks by congratulating ourselves that the hon. gentleman had not so far-although I do not know what he will do to-morrow or next week-charged the Government with responsibility for the war itself. He may endeavour to transfer the blame from the Kaiser to this Government or to the Minister of Finance, who is humbly endeavouring to do his duty in this great crisis. My hon. friend referred to the fact that we had a revenue this year of $100,000,000 more than we had in 1915, and he said that was no subject of congratulation. Well, I think that it is a real subject of congratulation; it means that the credit of Canada has been maintained. My hon. friend overlooks the fact that of all the belligerent countries at war, with the -single exception of the United States, the credit of Canada stands the highest. Would our credit stand as high as it does if our revenues were the same as they were in 1915? We have taken such measures since -the war broke out as have increased our revenues to $232,000,000. We have paid all current expenditure, all capital expenditure, all increased interest charges, and all pension chargee, and in addition have paid $60,000,000 on account of the principal of our war expenditures. My hon. friend says: You deserve no credit for that; there is no cause for congratulation in that fact. What, then, would call for congratulation? Upon what set of facts or conditions could congratulation be offered? I venture to say that any country of the world in which this financial statement was presented would s-ay that Canada had done well. And they are saying in New York and in London that Canada has don-e well. The highest tribute has been paid to the financial methods employed by this country since the war broke out, which are recognized as being of a most scientific character. They are saying this in Canadian

financial circles and among the public generally; the only place where it is not toeing said is among hon. gentlemen opposite. I am content to take the judgment of London, of New York and of the financial and business community and the general public of Canada, even as against the criticism of the hon. member for Edmonton.
My hon. friend says that there are no evidences of development in cities, and he suggests that the Government does not realize that we are at war. What does my hon. friend expect of a country at war? Does he expect to see buildings going up, when the price of material is 50 or 60 per cent higher than it was in times of peace and wihen the prices paid for labour are as high as they are at present? Take the city of Toronto as an example: every house, so far as I know, is rented at a good rental. Not much building is going on, because the energies of the country are directed to the prosecution of the war-and this is true not only of Canada, but of the other allied nations as well. Is this Government to be held responsible because real estate booms are lacking in the cities of Toronto and Montreal-engaged, as we are now, in the greatest war in history? Is that a fair argument, I ask my hon, friend? He says that agriculture is not developing. He says: you had a certain acreage under cultivation in 1911, an increased acreage in 1912, a diminished increase in the acreage of 1913, and, at present, a diminished increase in the acreage under cultivation in the West.
What would you expect with a war on calling for the man power of the country, with 400,000 men in this country called to the colours? I want to say to the hon. member for Edmonton and to every other hon. member and to every man in the country that, notwithstanding everything that can be said, this Government and, in particular, the people of this country deserve the greatest possible credit for the mighty effort which they have put forth in this war. In Canada, over 400,000 men have enlisted. What would be the corresponding effort in the United States which has thirteen times onr population? The corresponding effort on their part would be the enlistment of 5,000,000 men. We have raised those 400,000 men in a country geographically as large as Europe and with a population of 8,000,000 people of diverse nationalities. That has been the effort of the people of this country under the administration of this Government, and there is absolutely no room for national self-depreciation. I say that

to all times it will be a matter of pride on the part of the people of this country that Canada, in the three years of this war, has put forth the mighty effort in men that she has put forth.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext: Why then, do gentlemen on the other side encourage people to say that Canada is in default?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext: Then it must be so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext: I will not say it must be so, but it is very strong evidence that it is so if I said it.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext: That is what I was attempting to emphasize.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext: I am sorry I would not be able to .pay quite the same testimony to my hon. friend.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext: I will not mind that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext:
If I made that statement it is very strong prima facie evidence that it is true. My hon. friend said: You have nothing to congratulate yourself on the fact that you have a total trade of $2,000,000,000. Why not? Is it not real money? Before this war broke out the Balance of trade against Canada was between two and three hundred million dollars a year. That whole situation has since been reversed, and in terms of money. The balance of trade to-day is in our favour to the extent of $400,000,000. The point I make is that if our exports are worth more money the people have that money. My hon. friend seems !to hold the view that if the prices of commodities are higher than they were in normal times there is no advantage derived from that by the producer. But that, I believe, is not the case. Therefore, as I have stated, the argument of my hon. friend that the country is not to be congratulated upon its increased financial strength, upon its increased international trade and upon the increased value of its production generally, must fall to the ground. When this war broke out members of this Government, including myself, impressed upon the people of this country the necessity of production, more production and yet more production. That necessity has been continually drawn to the attention of the people of Canada, and I am happy to say that they have realized that necessity, and I think they would have realized it quite apart from the admonitions we gave them. But we did impress upon them the value of production, more production and again more production, and I believe it is by increasing production and by the exercise of national economy and national thrift that Canada, notwithstanding the war and the consequent increase in her national debt has been able to accomplish what I have mentioned to the House.

My hon. friend speaks of the tariff. He wants the tariff revised downwards. He has no belief in the tariff. He wishes to supply the revenues of this country by direct taxation. The inference from the remarks of my hon. friend from Edmonton and my hon. friend from Medicine Hat is that -we could practically do away with the tariff and raise all the money that is required for the expenditure of this country by direct taxation.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext: I understood the minister to say that I and the hon. member for Medicine Hat had taken the position that there should be no tariff. I think the minister will find that that statement is not borne out by what I said.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext:
Possibly my hon. friend did not say that there should be no tariff, nor do I recollect that I said he said that. I said that my hon. friend has no belief in the tariff. He brings forward a resolution for the revision of the tariff downwards. But his utterances in this House to-day and for a long time past go to convince me that he would rather the revenues of this country were raised by direct taxation, and that we practically had no tariff at all. Let me say that no matter how desirable that might be to my 'hon. friend we need not seriously consider it, because we simply could not raise the money that is required for the purposes of the Government, unless we had the tariff. The tariff is the main-stay of the revenues of this country, and must continue to be so, so far as I can see for an indefinite time to come.
We were speaking yesterday about income taxation, and my hon. friend from Medicine Hat has referred to it again to-day. It is easy to say that we could raise large sums of money by income taxation. Last night I sent a telegram to Mr. Bradshaw, Commissioner of Finance for the City of Toronto, I asked him what was the income assessment in the city of Toronto and how much they derived from it last year. Now, the city of Toronto is the second city in Canada, and there would probably be more income there liable to assessment than in the rest of the province of Ontario, and possibly also in one or more of the western provinces. We must remember that income is subject to taxation by the municipality of the city of Toronto with an exemption, I think, of $1,000, to a municipal tax of 20 to 25 mills on the dollar which is a little over 2 per cent. The reply I got from Mr. Bradshaw was that Toronto's income assessment in 
1916 was $19,500,000, and the amount of income tax raised was $440,000. I lay those figures before the House without comment. They seem to be very illuminating as to the possibilities of income taxation. I stated yesterday, and I repeat again to-day, that I think it very probable that the Dominion Government may have to resort to income taxation if this war goes on, and at the present moment there does not seem to be very much evidence of an early conclusion.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext: Will the income taxation displace any other taxation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext:
I do not think it well to make announcements with respect to taxation so far in advance. I stated that if the war went on we should have to consider new modes of taxation, and that we might resort to the income tax.
My hon. friend has referred to the production of munitions, and he did not seem to think that the industry was of very much consequence to this country. I can tell him that from two standpoints the production of munitions is of the utmost consequence. In the first place the munitions business in Canada has reached dimensions that exceed, I believe, those of any other business on this continent, excepting possibly one or two of the largest American businesses and I do not know that I should except those. There are some 650 establishments in Canada making munitions. It was of the utmost importance to the Imperial Government that they were able to lay under requisition the industrial establishments of this country for the purpose of supplementing the British supply of munitions. The economic justification for the establishment and promotion of industries in this country has often been referred Ito. The industries which were of economic value in time of peace become real bulwarks of national security in time of war. All the industries of this country have been laid under requisition by the Imperial Government, and have been sending forward munitions on an increasing scale for the last two years. I think it is nolt too much to say that the supply of munitions which has gone from this country in an unending stream for the last two years has had much to do with the successful operations pn the Somme, at Vimy Ridge and other points on (the western front. So it was a great thing for this country from the standpoint of the prosecution of the war, that Canadian industrial plants were able to send forward in increasingly large quantities the munitions so urgently required at the front.

But apart from that, there is the economic value to Canada. Hundreds of thousands of people are engaged in the munitions business in this country; they are paid for their services, -and in that way there has been a large distribution of money in Canada which has had a very considerable effect upon our economy. These munitions were needed; the British Government was willing to pay for them, and the business has been developed to the extent I have indicated. From an economic standpoint the industry has been of great benefit to the people of this country, but I consider that of secondary importance. The main thing is that we had the industrial plants to supply the Shells and other munitions so urgently needed at the front.
My hon. friend seems to censure this Government; he has no word of praise for what the Government has done. I am indifferent whether we get praise or blame, so long as the work is done, but I will put forward for the consideration of the House that we have financed in large measure the expenditure which has made possible the manufacture of munitions in this country on such a large scale. The hon. member for Edmonton has said that we have no industries in process of expansion in Canada. Well, the country is engaged in war; the manpower of the country is being organized. In those circumstances, how can my hon. friend expect an expansion of business other than in industries connected directly or indirectly with the war? Was that a reasonable criticism of the Government? I submit not. My hon. friend says that we get too much from the tariff, and we are not taking enough from excess profits. Last night hon. gentlemen opposite censured the Government because the excess profits tax was too heavy. To-day, the hon. member for Edmonton says that the excess profits tax is much too light. Instead of raising $12,500,000 in 1915, and $20,000,000 in 1916, he would probably "guess," like my hon. friend from Dauphin, that we should raise $100,000,000 from excess profits. He had no figures to support his argument. He simply made the statement that we were not raising enough money from the excess profits, I would point out that this Government must not only raise revenue to meet its ordinary and capital expenditure, the interest upon its increasing debt, and the pensions, but we must have a large revenue in order to maintain our credit.
In 1916, we raised the tariff 7i per cent and 5 per cent. It was stated at the time, and actually moved as an amendment in the Budget debate, that the House should put itself on record as declaring that the tax would not be productive. So productive has that tax been that I was able to say yesterday that the increase due to the war tax had been last year $38,000,000, and for the previous year $25,000,000. If ever there was a prophecy that was not fulfilled, it was the prediction of hon. gentlemen opposite in 1915 that we should realize no additional revenue by the increase in the tariff. To-day we find ourselves in th^ position, as to credit, as to financial standing and power, which I have indicated, and this is due largely to the fact that we met conditions as they arose from time to time, that we imposed the measure of taxation necessary in order to meet our coming requirements.
I would point out to my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) that in the United States Congress to-day there is a measure to increase the tariff all around by ten per cent. I do not know what progress that measure has made. It was introduced, I believe, by the Ways and Means Committee, or at least it was the proposal put forward by the Ways and Means Committee for the raising of additional revenue for the United States to meet the requirements of the war.
The hon. member has asserted that this Government has increased the burden of taxation on the people of Canada. He puts that forward as a serious indictment of the Government. Of course, we have increased the burden of taxation on the people of Canada. Why? It certainly is not because we desire to increase the people's burden for the mere sake of doing so; it is the result of necessity arising out of the war. The measures we have taken have been such, I believe, as command themselves to the judgment of the people throughout the country.
The hon. member seems to think that the Government is not interested in the West. He spoke of the duty on agricultural implements. When I asked him, pointblank, *why it was that when he was a member of the late Government he did not take the duty off agricultural implements, his answer was, "I don't know." I do not believe that is a sufficient answer. In the tariff of 1914, we reduced the duties on many of those implements in which the West is particularly interested-" harvesters, self-binders,

reapers and parts thereof," to quote the tariff item. The duty on these machines was cut down to 124 per cent. During all the time when the Government of which the hon. member for Edmonton was a member was in power the duties on these implements had been 174 per cent. And he thought he had worked wonders because under the reciprocity agreement the duty was fixed at 15 per cent. This Government, which the ;hon. gentleman says has no interest in the western farmer, fixed these duties, not at the 174 per cent at which he was quite content to have it when in power, %not at the 15 per cent fixed by the reciprocity agreement which he has never ceased to praise in this House, but at 124 per cent. And when we raised the tariff two years ago the increase did not apply to these agricultural implements. I think I have proved that my hon. friend is not quite sincere in bringing forward this motion. If he indicts this Government for not dealing with the question of agricultural implements he must explain to his constituents why, when he was in power, he did not do what he now says this Government ought to do.
The hon. member spoke about the wheat. He said that the farmers in the West had sold out at $1.75 a bushel. When he was asked how much wheat the farmers had in store, either on their farms or in elevators, he said he did not know. He had taken no trouble to inquire. I believe, in fact I know, that it is incorrect to say that the farmers of the West sold out all their wheat at $1.75 a bushel.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext: I did not say they sold it all out at $1.75.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman did not say so, at least he created that impression. He was asked how much the farmers had in store-

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext: I said that nobody knows.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext:
But the hon. gentleman created the impression that the farmers of the West by reason of a conspiracy-which he practically alleged-between the railways, the Board of Railway Commissioners and the grain manipulators, were actually deprived of the difference between $1.75 a bushel and $3 a bushel. If he did not intend to create that impression he succeeded in doing that which he had not intended to do. That is the impression he created in this House, and I think it is the impression he intended t'o create. He left out of account the myriad transactions in wheat in Chicago, in Minneapolis, in

Duluth. He said somebody made $70,000,000. Why, all interests throughout the world are concerned in, the buying of that grain from the time it leaves the farm to the time it leaves the elevators. Yet he blames the Government by implication, because we did not stop that mysterious somebody from making that $70,000,000. Who have been the great buyers of this grain? The British Wheat Commission. The British Government. It was the buying of the British Government that was particularly the cause of what has been called the corner in wheat.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext: Oh, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext: I know it.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext: It was the selling by men who had not the wheat.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is wrong. The British Wheat Commission bought in perfect good faith and with no intention of creating a corner-

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext: Certainly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext:
The men who
bought wheat in the ordinary course sold in the ordinary course, by what is known as "hedging."

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext: They sold wheat that they did not have and could not get.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext: But the hon. gentleman knows that in the course of business that is done.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext: That is what they did.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext: They bought the grain and they were obliged to "hedge"- that is, they were obliged to sell. They sold in the ordinary course that is pursued in this country, in the United States, and, so far as I know, in every other country. They sold expecting that if tne contract grades could not be supplied, they would be allowed to substitute grades at millable value. But the British Government, for reasons that I have already referred to, wanted the grades 1, 2 and 3, and not the lower grades.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext: Anybody who buys as the British Commission bought expects to buy nothing but contract grades.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext: I understand. But these men sold, as I have stated, in good faith.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext:
They had no right to sell
anything but contract grades.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext:
Let me show my hon. friend that he is quite wrong. When

this corner was formed-due, as I have said, to the buying iby tihe British Wheat Commission in perfect good faith and in such immense 'quantities that the ordinary laws, so to eay, went by the board-and wheat attained the price it did two or three weeks ago, we took the matter up at once with the British Wheat Commission. I cabled Sir George Perley asking him to take the matter up with the British Wheat .Commission. I took it up with the representative of the British Wheat Commission at Washington. I know what I am talking about. Just as soon as it was determined that they would accept the lower grade in lieu of contract grades, which they were entitled to demand, the corner came to an end.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext: And the Government arranged to let the wheat speculator out.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext:
Now, my hon.
- friend puts that forward seriously in this House. Here were the British Wheat Commission buying millions and tens of millions of bushels of wheat for the sustenance of the people of the United Kingdom. As a result of that buying, and as a result of innumerable contracts made on the Winnipeg exchange, and in Minneapolis and Chicago, wheat goes to a certain price and yet my hon. friend says that the Government, or the Railway Commission, and the railways are in a conspiracy against the farmers of the West. If that is not an absolute reductio ad absurdum I do not know what it Is.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext: Under the circumstances, seeing that a comer had 'been created, did this Government take any steps under the War Measures Act to control the price?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext:
My hon. friend
puts forward his usual insidious question. My hon. friend has a lot to leam about wheat if he does not know the dependence there is between wheat on the Winnipeg Exchange, wheat on the Chicago Exchange and wheat on the Minneapolis Exchange.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext: I know very well that this Government have the power, and that they had the power then, to control the price of wheat and k-eep it within reasonable limits.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext:
My hon. friend
puts that forward and if the Government had done it my hon. friend would have come forward and suggested some other line of action, so that we are perhaps as far ahead in any event. The Government
took the only action it could take in respect to the situation. The Government cannot control the world prices of wheat. My hon. friend knows that.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext:
But it could control
the Canadian price.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext: The Government of the United States could not control the world price of wheat.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext: They could control the price in their own country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext: They cannot even do that. The only possibility of controlling the minimum or maximum price-and the subject is full of difficulties-would be by joint action on the part of the two governments. That is recognized in the United States just as it is here. We might as well talk sense about this.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext: Will my hon. friend not get angry if I ask him another question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext: Could any one get angry with the hon. gentleman?

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext: If the Canadian Government could not control the price of wheat in Canada, how is it possible for Canada and the United States to control the price of wheat in these two countries when we know that wheat is produced largely in Argentine and other countries of the world?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext:
If my hon. friend had an open mind I would have no difficulty in answering his question but he has a mens clausa, a closed mind, I am afraid that I cannot give the hon. gentleman the answer that he wants. However, I shall try to reply to my hon. friend. My hon. friend knows the close connection geographically between this country and the United States and the tonnage situation on the Atlantic which affects Argentina, Australia, New Zealand and all other sources of supply-
Now, I come to this amendment. The amendment suggests a revision of the Customs tariff. My hon. friend (Mr. Oliver) acquiesces in that and he says: I want a revision now and I want a revision downward. If there ever was a time in the history of Canada when it was unwise to revise the tariff, it is this present moment. What is the condition? The condition, Mr. Speaker, is that owing to the unsettled values of goods in all foreign countries, it would be -absolutely impossible to prepare a customs tariff that would meet the situation at the present time and for a period

after the war. A proper revision of the tariff to-day would be an impossible performance, and would lead to the most profound dislocation of business in this country at a time when the last thing we want to see is the dislocation of business. Yet, my hon. friend from Edmonton seriously suggests that this Government, in the midst of this war, should revise the tariff. The wholesale values of two hundred commodities in the United States have increased by 65 per cent up to March, 1917, in comparison with the prices in July, 1914. I pointed out that the present Customs tariff is producing a very large revenue. That revenue is needed and it is going to be needed in increasing amount until the war is over. We shall have to face, as the United States had, the problems arising out of the war, an enormous increase in the national	debt,	interest	charges
and pension outlays and my hon. friend suggests that you can practically put the tariff out of consideration in dealing with these questions. How did the United States meet the situation, and no country ever recovered from a great war so successfully as the United States. How did the United States put herself upon a gold basis after the war? A dollar in 1863 was worth only about 40 cents in gold.. How did the United States bring her dollar to parity, how did the United States not only meet the interest upon her great national debt but pay off that debt in a few years? She did it by the tariff. This country cannot dispense with the tariff at this time. I do not say that the tariff is perfect. I do not say that at the proper time the tariff should not be revised, but I do say that it is idle to suggest that you can get on without a tariff. At this time it would be unwise in the extreme to revise the tariff.
If it is unwise to revise the tariff, we need not seriously consider the question of revising the tariff downwards. The tariff was increased in 1915 by 7| per cent and 5 per cent. In the course of time, I should imagine when the war is about over, it will be necessary to revise the tariff. I do not say it should be revised upwards, I do not say it should be revised downwards, but I say it should be revised having regard to the conditions that exist at the time of its revision. If a tariff revision takes place it will have to be necessarily in the light of the Situation which exists as between the- Allies in this war. There may be trade conventions; there undoubtedly will be treaties between the Allies.

That is the general opinion and, if so, why should we revise our tariff now when the war is moving, we hope, towards its close, and when the situation that I have indicated will confront us at the conclusion of the war? What we should do is to maintain our tariff because it gives the revenues which are necessary for the purposes of the country and the prosecution of the war. At the proper time, on the conclusion of the war, and having regard to the situation which then exists, including the international situation between the Allies, be proper for us to revise the tariff. We shall know the labour and the industrial situation and the fiscal measures we take will be such as are in the public interest. I shall not discuss the question of placing wheat, flour, and wheat products on the free list. That has been done as to-

My hon. friend has referred also to the British preference. Well, it is not expedient to deal with the tariff at the present time or with the British preference; but, when the war is over, when this question of preference, about which the Prime Minister spoke the other day, ,and which has been under consideration by the Imperial War Cabinet, is before the Government, and when we know the industrial situation that confronts us and the world, and when we have before us the agreements made between the Allies, we can deal with this and all other questions in such fashion as the interests of Canada and the Empire may require.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I crave the indulgence of the r House for a short time this evening to discuss what I consider to be one of the most important resolutions that has been proposed to the House in recent years. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance will not feel that I am discourteous if I do not follow him through all the by-ipaths and by-ways that he trod this afternoon, because, for some unexplainable reason, he took occasion to deliver to-day the same speech that he has repeated four or five times during the last three weeks. Possibly he felt sufficient justification for the performance; I hope that he is satisfied with the results. Before I enter upon a discussion of the real question involved in the amendment, however, I desire to refer very shortly to a few of the more outstanding statements made by the Minister of Finance.
When the history of this country is written, one thing that my hon. friend will not be charged with is a lack of due appreciation of his own services and of the services of his party. Outside of winning the war, I do not know of anything for which the hon. gentleman did not take credit this afternoon in a speech of one hour's duration. The Minister of Finance even went so far as to say that the successes in the battles of the Somme and Vimy Ridge were contributed to very largely by the immediate action taken by the Government in the matter of furnishing rails. One can almost say, therefore, that the hon. gentleman is taking credit for the winning of the war, as
well as for almost everything else in the world. He said that the Government deserved very great credit for the mighty efforts that they had put forth towards the winning of the war. Mighty efforts? Well, he and his Government have done a great many things since the war started. I assume that my hon. friend is willing to take credit for everything that has been done,, but for some of those things he is not entitled to a great deal of credit. Let me refer to a few of the things that he has done and for which he takes to himself so much credit.
The minister says that the Government have placed the finances of Canada in a better position than those of any other country in the wprld except the United States. He glories in the assertion, which he has made a great many times during the last three weeks, that when the Government wanted money from the Canadian people they were able to get it. When they wanted $59,000,000 they were offered $100,000,000; when they wanted $100,000,000 they were offered $200,000,000; when they wanted $150,000,000 they were -offered$260,000,-000. He said that he did not believe $5,000,000 could have been raised by loan in Canada before the war. But he did not tell us that no other Canadian Government had ever tried to raise -an internal loan. He did not tell us that during the years from 1867 to 1915 the successive Governments of Canada deliberately and persistently went outside the borders of our country in order to raise money. This matter was discussed when my hon. friend's predecessor held office, as well as since the present Government came into power. I myself have more than once asked why the Government did not attempt to raise money by internal loan, and the answer was always the same: in <a young country like Canada it was better to borrow money from outside than to tie up money of our own which was needed for the country's development. Accordingly, up to the year 1915 the Government never offered more than three ,per cent for money obtained in Canada; yet under the system of paying three per cent interest on savings bank deposits, hundreds of millions of dollars were deposited to the credit of the Government. But pne of the most gigantic efforts for which the Minister of Finance takes credit is the raising of money in Canada. And how was this wonderful feat accomplished? By raising the interest rate from three per cent to five per cent and then selling bonds cheap enough to give

the broker a small commision on the sale of bonds. Nobody but a real wizard of finance could do that. Does the minister realize that hundreds of millions of dollars were lying around this country before he took charge of the Finance Department? Does he realize that nearly $100,000,000 were deposited in the Dominion Savings Bank, and much more than $200,000,000 or $300,000,000 in the chartered banks at three per cent interest?' Does he realize that hundreds of millions of dollars, earning no interest at all, were in the chartered banks, and that there were in Canada securities to the value of hundreds of millions of dollars bearing only 3, 3J or 4 per cent interest? Does he realize that the moment he raised the rate of interest to 5 per cent every woman who had money in a savings bank, every investor who had money lying round for which he was not receiving 5 per cent interest, came to the conclusion that by placing their money with the Government at 5 per cent, backed by the security of the Government, they would be making a pretty good trade? The minister admitted that one night last week when he said that a variation of one-tenth of a point would have defeated his purpose. He admitted that the money was obtained not by his financing but by his offering an increased rate of interest and a method of investment which caused the people to come fofivard with their money. Yet he says that the Government is entitled to the very greatest credit for the raising of $300,000,000 through internal loans under these conditions.
My hon. friend (Sir Thomas White) says, also, that the Government deserve an enormous amount of credit because they attracted such large sums of money into the country in connection with the manufacture of munitions. Well, the Government are welcome to all the credit they can get for the money that has come in for the manufacture of munitions. The late Minister of Militia takes all the credit for that to himself, but I happen to know something about this matter; I spent some time trying to find out about it. The Government so mismanaged the thing that the British authorities said: if you cannot manufacture these munitions at reasonable prices you shall not be permitted to manufacture at all. So they had to take the matter out of the hands of the Government, and put it into the hands of a board constituted by themselves. The British Government have spent, perhaps, a billion dollars in Canada since the outbreak of war for the purchase of munitions, but I

do not see how the Government can take any credit for that. The allied armies were suffering from a lack of munitions of war more than anything else; they had to have them; they paid two prices for every dollar's worth of munitions they got from Canada, except, perhaps, for the munitions which they have obtained during the last six months or year. Many people in Canada are hiding their heads in shame because they had the nerve to charge the British and allied Governments the prices that they did. They charged such prices that the British Government were compelled, as I say, to send their representatives here and take the business out of their hands. Yet, hon. gentlemen opposite claim to be entitled to all credit for the manufacture of munitions in Canada.
My hon. friend says, further, that the tariff should not be revised during a period of war. But it did not bother my hon. friend to revise the tariff in 1914, when he added a few million dollars to the taxes.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext: That was upward.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS TARIFF.
speechtext:
Yes, but he revised it just the same. It did not bother him in 1915, when he raised the tariff 7i per cent and 5 per cent. It did not bother him a year ago, when his colleague the Minister of Agriculture, wanting a better price for his apples, put 75 cents duty on each barrel of apples coming into Canada, making the farmer of the West pay that much more for his apples than he had ever paid before. It is a simple matter for my hon. friend to revise the tariff upwards, but when he is asked to revise the tariff downwards and relieve the almost impossible burden upon the poor man who is trying to make a living he says that it is impossible to do it until the war is over.
The minister says that we have raised $60,000,000 or thereabouts by way of special taxes. It is a very simple matter to raise $60,000,000 in special taxes when you add 7h and 5 per cent duty to the price of everything that the people bring into the countrv.
It is not only five and seven and a half per cent duty that you add. When you consider that the articles which are being brought in to this country are not very much greater in volume than they were before the war, but that they are in some cases twice the value and in some cases even three times the value, and when to the tariff as it was before the war, you add 5 per cent in one case and 7i per cent in the other on a value in dollars two or three times as great as it was before, you are not doing

a wonderful feat of financing in order to get additional revenue out of the people of Canada. I do not think the Minister of Finance is entitled to as much credit for raising this money as he thinks he is; but, of course, I know he has a right to his own opinion. I want, however, to point out some of the ways in which I feel he would be benefitting the people of this country if he were to adopt this amendment in his method of raising a revenue.
The Minister of Finance *told the House the wonderful things the Government had done in stimulating production, but he failed to tell us the manner in which they had endeavoured to stimulate production. He said that they were constantly preaching production and more production. What have they done? Have they done anything towards producing more grain, more food, more cattle? The only thing I know which they have ever done was done within the last two months, when they put wheat on the free list, but up to the present time there has not been very much result so far as increased production is concerned. We hope, however, that measure will have; in this coming year and in later years, the effect of stimulating the production of wheat, and so far as that is concerned, we are willing to give the minister full credit for what he has done. That, however, is a matter which, properly, I think should have been discussed upon the Budget and which was discussed upon the Budget by my hon. friend and by many other members of the House; and as I said at the beginning of my remarks, I am not going to take up time discussing matters which should have been discussed on the Budget, but I am going to confine my remarks to the resolutions and the amendment before the House.
In asking the House to adopt this amendment we are raising a very vital question in Canada; we are raising a question of principle, which I am sorry to say has not been discussed in this House during the last fifteen years as much as it should have been. It is a question of principle that has been forgotten in Canada for a good many years and that should be revived now on account of the war, if foT no other reason. My hon. friend saye:	You
cannot revise a tariff during the war; you have to havie more money and you must raise it by means of a tariff. There never has been a time in the history of Canada when you can revise the tariff downward as well as you can to-day. There has never

been a time when you can discuss the question. of the tariff with the people of Canada as well as you can to-day. Down to the beginning of the war things had been going fairly well; the people were fairly prosperous; we did not have to raise very much money; our taxes were low; we did not know as much as the people of other countries do about raising money; and when you discussed the question of direct taxation, there is no doubt that a great outcry would be raised against it, but the people have learned that you cannoit raise a very large revenue by means of a tariff, notwithstanding that my hon, friend says that a tariff must, for many years, be the great means by which revenue shall be raised. He himself has adopted a policy of raising money in other ways than by a tariff. Supposing any Minister of Finance had before the war attempted to raise money by a business tax, as my hon. friend is doing now, one can quite understand what an outcry there would have been against it. My hon. friend, however, is raising money by means of a business tax, >and the only criticism I have heard in regard to' it is (that he is not raising enough by it. For the last month we have been persistently telling the Minister of Finance that he must raise money by means of an income tax, and he has been, until this afternoon, persistently telling us that he cannot do it. Now he says: I am wrong. I think I can raise money by means of an income tax, and I guess I shall have to do so. That shows that even a hidebound tariff politician like the Minister of Finance has lucid intervals, and if you im press truths upon him long enough and persistently enough, even he comes to his senses and has to admit that these matters are not so entirely theoretical as he would try to lead the House to believe.' This afternoon he said: Yes, we shall have to impose an income tax, I am fraid, but iit will not produce anything, because I sent a telegram to the controller at Toronto and that gentleman replied: "We collected only half a million dollars or a little less of an income tax last year." My hon. friend certainly, looks upon the members of this House as being very unsophisticated in the methods of taxation for municipal purposes in Canada. He speaks about collecting only half a million dollars from an income tax in the city of Toronto. I do not suppose that one-half or one-third of the incomes in the city of Toronto that are above $1,000 are taxed at all. If they are, Toronto is different from any other city or town in Canada

that I know of. In my own province of New Brunswick we have an income tax for municipal purpose's, and in that province there is not a man but, when he looks at the item of income tax on his tax bill, simply laughs in his sleeve to think of the small amount of income upon which he is assessed, and what is true of my province is true of the province of Ontario. The minister also admits that the tax only amounts to 2 per cent. A man with an income of $50,000 is assessed as having an income of $2,000, and then he is charged 2 per cent on $2,000 or a tax of the paltry sum of say $40. My hon. friend knows that if he went after the big incomes of this country as is done in Great Britain, France, and many other countries, he would be taxing the rich man, not 2 per cent of his income, but from 30 to 40 per cent of his income, and he knows that in Great Britain there are people who are paying as high as 40 per cent of their incomes. Let my hon. friend adopt a system of a graduated income tax as has been done in other civilized countries, and let him take the matter up in a big way and he will collect, not half a million dollars from Toronto, but three .or four million dollars, and he will collect proportionate amounts from every other city and town throughout the Dominion. My hon. friend might just as well come down the whole way on this question of income tax and admit to himself and to the country that an income tax is coming; that it is a proper method of raising a revenue, and that it is not a serious matter at all, because it is not a novelty; it is not something that has not been worked out. It has been worked out to perfection in many countries in the world, and all that my hon. friend has to do is to adopt that method which in his judgment best applies to the condition of affairs in Canada and to apply it. If he does that, he will get money just as easily and much more fairly than he is doing by raising the duty 7} per cent on the poor man who can barely make both ends meet and at the same time buy sufficient food and clothing for his family.
There is, however, another side to this question which, in my judgment, the Minister of Finance fails to consider, and which I think, my hon. friends opposite fail to consider when they are discussing this question of tariff. They say: Oh, but if you reduce the tariff, you will not have any revenue; you have to have a revenue in

order to carry on this war, and the only way to secure that revenue is to keep up the tariff. I want to tell my hon. friend, in the first place, that that has not been the history of Canada, nor of any other country in the world. We know that in 1897 when the British J preference was introduced in this country, j which meant an enormous reduction in the tariff, the tariff revenue did not decrease, but went up by leaps and bounds at the rate of $10,000,000 a year. It is all very simple. The moment you take the duty off any article-I do not ask that everything be put on tlhe free list, but I say reduce the duty-the moment you reduce the duty on an article of ordinary consumption, that moment you make it cheaper, and you put the average consumer in a better position' to purchase. If he purchases more, then more goods come into the country, and more revenue comes into the coffers of the Government; that is a general principle which I do not think anybody will dispute.
But there is another side to it. My hon. friend fails to tell the House, though he knows it as well as any man in Canada, that our tariff with the 7j per cent added to it, is in many cases so high that it absolutely prohibits the importation of the necessities of life; that is the difficulty. Instead of getting revenue you get none at all, because the duty is prohibitive, and at the same time you are increasing the burdens of the people by-100 per cent I was going to say, and I believe in many : cases it amounts to that. You get no revenue, and you increase the cost to the consumer, because you have built up the tariff wall to such an extent that the consumer j cannot import, and is compelled to buy j from the local producer at a price which j is just a cent or two below the imported | article. I think perhaps the most glaring instance of that in the whole of our trade returns is the item of cement. I was amazed in looking over the trade returns for the year ending March 31, 1916, to see the figures for thifl item. I was not able to get the returns beyond that date, and .therefore any figures I may quote this evening will have reference to the fiscal year ending March 31, 1916. According to the trade returns, we neither bought nor sold cement with the rest of the world; we simply lived within ourselves. Hon. gentlemen opposite said in 1911, " Let us trade within ourselves; do not let us go beyond our own borders; do not tear down the flag; do not become disloyal by trading outside

this country, but let us just live within ourselves, and keep this little circle going," and, if ever there was an item where this idea was worked out to perfection it was in the case of ,our trade in cement last year, because the whole of Canada imported only $45,000 worth of cement, and we exported only $5,000 worth. We paid in duty the immense sum of $11,227 and if you add the 74 per cent you have $2,000 more. Altogether we paid abput $14,000 duty on cement. I do not know how many million dollars worth of cement is produced in Canada annually, but I do know that it would be a very great amount. I am very much of the opinion that it must be $20,000,000 or $30,000,000 worth; that is only an estimate, but the figure must be very, very large. But no matter whether it is $10,000,000 or $20,000,000 or $30,000,000 we are paying the manufacturers of cement in Canada practically 60 cents a barrel more than we should have to pay if we could import cement duty free. If the duty were taken off, the country would lose practically no revenue, but the consumer would be able' to buy cement for 60 cents a barrel less. I think that is perhaps the most glaring case in the trade returns, but there is another case nearly as bad. It is an article which every man and every woman in this country consumes, and the poorer the man the more he consumes of it. I refer tp canned vegetables. Perhaps there is no item of food in the Dominion to-day that plays a bigger part in the homes of the poor people than the tw.o canned vegetables which are bracketed together in the trade returns, tomatoes and cooked com. You would hardly believe it, Sir, but last year we received in duty on these two great articles in the diet of the common people the sum of $6,454 .only; in addition	to	that
straight duty, there would be the war tax of 74 per cent, provided the goods came from any country outside the British Empire, which I presume they did. In this case again, the tariff is so high that we cannot import canned goods into this country. We simply have to pay the canners' combine the price which they ask, and that price is just a fraction of a cent below what the goods cost in any other country plus the duty. The poor man is accordingly compelled to pay to these people, I do not know how many hundreds of thousands or millions of dollars more than he would have to pay if these goods were on the free list, and if they were on 1084
the free list the revenue of Canada would only suffer to the extent of $6,454.
The next item is pretty nearly as important, but perhaps not so glaring as the two items of cement and canned goods. I come next to boots and shoes. Why, Sir, you cannot buy a pair of shoes in Canada to-day for your baby at less than $2 or $3 a pair, or for your child at less than $5 or $6, and you cannot buy a pair for yourself at less than $8 or $10. I realize that this is due in some measure to the increased cost of labour and production and to war prices; I want to be fair in arguing this question, for if a man is not fair in logic his argument amounts to nothing. We pay 374 per cent protection on the boots and shoes we buy in Canada. The duty is so great that only a mere bagatelle of the boots and shoes we use in Canada are purchased from outside. I do not know exactly what the consumption would be, but there are about 7,500,000 people in this country, and I think about $5 a head is a very low estimate for boots and shoes; in fact, I think that is away below the actual figure. But at $5 a head, we are paying $40,000,000 a year for boots and shoes, and yet, according to the trade returns, we imported only $2,120,000 worth, and these would all be shoes of the higher grade, slippers and things of that kind from England, although a large quantity come from the United States. But 90 per cent of the boots and shoes used in Canada are made at home. Under our tariff we are compelled to pay 374 per cent to the manufacturer of these boots and shoes, and last year we only received in revenue $775,000, including the 74 per cent. Just think of it! Only three-quarters of a million dollars of revenue on a consumption of $40,000,000 to $50,000,000 worth of boots and shoes ! Yet hon. gentlemen opposite tell us that we have to have this tariff to raise money to carry on the war. The Minister of Finance knows these things as well as I do. He knows all about these glaring inconsistencies, and how the poor man is being mulcted to make the rich man richer and to multiply our millionaires, but in discussing the tariff he very conveniently conceals these facts from the public. I could give illustration after illustration of the same thing.
Last year we imported $19,664,000 worth 3f woollen goods-practically twenty millions of -dollars' worth. The duties paid on those goods ran up in some cases to 40

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
and even 42 per cent, and this on goods which the poor man must buy to clothe 'his family in this rigorous climate; without these goods, people can hardly live in Canada. And this is done in order to keep a _ few one-horse factories going in Canada. It would be better to close up every woollen mill in the country than to tax the people at this enormous rate for goods without which they cannot get along. But I do not want to close up any factory; it is not necessary. I would not advocate the placing on . | the free list of any article if I believed that | by so doing we should close up an industry I in Canada; but I would not allow any industry to exist, producing goods of vital ! necessity to the poor people of this country, if it were necessary to its existence to ^ compel the people to pay a fine to the manu-| faeturer of 40 to 45 per cent. If a woollen factory in Canada cannot get along with a protection of 15 to 20 per cent, I do not think that factory is very much good to this country. The only good reason for the Minister of Finance maintaining such a condition of affairs is the need of revenue.
I admit that by the duty on woollen goods we raise a large revenue-last year it amounted to practically $6,500,000. I realize that if you reduced the duty to one-half or one-third of what it is to-day, you might not get so large an amount, but you would import more woollen goods. We have reached a point where woollen goods are practically out of the reach of ordinary people, they simply have not the money to buy them. But put those goods at reasonable prices and you will find that many people will buy them who cannot buy them to-day. I have strong reason to believe that if you had only one-third of the duty that you have to-day you would get nearly as much revenue as you do under the present rate of duty. There would not be so many woollen factories that would have to water their stock in order to cover up their earnings. Nor would these watered securities be selling at the price they are^ to-day. But that would only make the millionaires a little less millionaires than they are now, while it would be a wonderful benefit to the consumers of this country.
There is another side to this whole nefarious transaction, and it is being emphasized in the conduct of this war more than it has ever been emphasized before. It brings us back to the item of cement, one of the most glaring instances of all. It is well known that there are securities of the Canada Cement Company in the 
form' of bonds. These are all right; they represent actual money on which interest should be paid. Then, there is a certain amount of preferred stock. This is in the doubtful class. But give it the benefit of the doubt; say that it represents cash- though I am very much of opinion that there is a good deal of water in it-and that dividends should be paid on it. Then you have $13,000,000 of absolute water in the form of common stock, which did not cost the promoters of the Canada Cement Company one dime. Up to the time of the war this stock was practically worthless. There was a little professional trading in it at around 21 and 22, but very little of the stock was filtering out on the market. The Canada Cement Company got a contract for manufacturing munitions; they got it under peculiar circumstances, circumstances which ought to make every member of the Government and every supporter of the Government hang his head in shame. The company wanted to manufacture a certain form of shell at $55. The powers that be said: we can't do that, but if you will take $68, we will give you a contract. The Cement Company said they did not want it at that, that they could manufacture the shell at profit at $55, and they wanted the contract at that figure. They had to take that to the Prime Minister of this Dominion and the representatives of the British Munitions Board in Canada, and, after putting up a fight for some weeks, they finally succeeded in compelling the powers that be_ to give them a contract at $55. And they have made so much money that the common stock is selling at 59 and 60; it has even been above that-I have not looked at the quotations for the last day or two. Large quantities of that stock are being sent broadcast over the country. It gets into the hands of men and women who have money to invest, and the company is earning so much money that it is beginning to pay dividends upon that watered stock. But wait until the war is over; wait until you want to reduce the price of cement; wait until you wish to take the duty off cement, when things are not in the flourishing condition they are in to-day, and see what the owners of this watered stock will say. They will say: We paid good cold cash for our stock, and if you take the duty off cement you are going to reduce the price of that stock to such an extent that we cannot pay dividends. In other words, you will 'be wiping out money which these people have paid in good faith, which they paid not knowing the conditions, which they paid

because of the fact that the Parliament of Canada is keeping a duty of sixty cents a barrel on cement. I cannot conceive of a greater crime to be perpetrated on the investing public of any country than to continue a condition of affairs such as I have described. And you have the same principle in boots and shoes. You have $3,000,000 or $4,000,000 of absolutely watered stock in Ames, Holden & McCready. That stock, before the war, was not worth two cents; you could not give it away; no man would pay for it what it would cost to transfer it in the books of the company. But this concern has contracts with the Government to furnish shoes by the million dollars' worth, and to-day this watered stock is filtering out to the ordinary investor 'at 15 and 16 cents a share. There is not very much going out yet, but it is going out, and if the present condition of affairs continues very much longer you will find a million dollars' worth of this stock scattered broadcast over the country. Then, when the time comes when you wish to take the duty off boots and shoes, the holders of that stock will say that you are making worthless a stock for which they paid money in good faith. So you are providing in advance a strong argument in favour of maintaining the duty on boots and shoes. If ever there was a time when these things should he grappled with firmly to-night is that time. There never was a time when you could introduce a system of direct taxation as easily as you can to-day. There never was a time when the industries of Canada were as flourishing or were making as much money as they are to-day; there never was a time when as much watered stock was being scattered broadcast over Canada as to-day, and there never was a time when it was more fitting that Parliament should take this matter in hand and make it impossible for these companies to sell for good money that which represents nothing to them in the way of money, that which is merely watered stock.
There is another very far-reaching principle involved in this amendment, one that has been discussed to a great extent in this House during the last three or four weeks, one On which the hon. gentlemen opposite have turned naarejolitical somersaults than in all their experience since the inception of the National Policy. I refer to their action in regard to wheat and flour. It is not a year ago-why, it is not two months ago-that the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) stated that the agitation for free wheat was nine-tenths political and one-tenth bad economics. And he even says
that now. I want to ask him, or to ask the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) why it was that, believing this statement of the hon. gentleman, they accepted the principle of free wheat. They told us that the adoption of free wheat was going to tear down the Union Jack from every flagpole in Canada and raise the Stars and Stripes in its place; that it was going to convert our railways into streaks of rust; that it was going to drive the trade of Canada to run north and south instead of east and west. If they were right in their contention, or even if they believed what they said-and what the Solicitor General says even now-what are we to think of men who will make such a volte face as that which they have made, and without any reason for it?
But, I tell you, Mr. Speaker, they did not believe in it in 1911. They knew that it would not remove the British flag from a .solitary flag pole in Canada, they knew it would not throw anybody out of employment and they knew they were putting *up the greatest hoax upon the people of Canada that was ever put up upon the people of any country. They knew it would ;not turn the railways into streaks of rust and they knew that it would not divert traffic from the railways running east and west to railways Tunning north and south. Hon. gentlemen opposite knew it, the railways knew it, the manufacturers knew it but yet they fooled the people and by that means they succeeded in getting into power. They had to pay back the people who put them in power by adding 7J per cent to the cost of everything that they produced when this war came on instead of trying to raise money by more modem and scientific methods. When you. ask them to do something to Temove that iniquity they say:	You cannot do it; you can only
raise money in war time by means of the tariff. But, they did remove the duty on wheat and I am very glad they have done so. I have reason to believe, from the intimation made by the Minister of Finance, that they intend to go farther and remove the duty from wheat products.

Sir THOiMAS WHITE:	My hon. friend

I am.
