Sir THOMAS W/HITE: Wheat products -that is the amendment before the House of the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver). What I stated was that the Government had placed upon the free list, wheat, wheat flour and semolina. That is done.

It is well to have this matter cleared up and to know that the minister does not intend to put wheat products on the free list by Order in Council. It is well that the men in this country who are trying to produce more should know that. The minister says: Production, and still more production; we want you to raise more cattle, more hogs; we want you to increase production if possible, hut we are going to make you pay $3, $4 or $5 more per ton for the food of these animals than you would have to pay if we took the duty off. It is well that the people should know also that the keeping on of that duty does not add one dollar to the revenues of ithe country. It is well that the people of this country who havie livestock should know what the attitude of the minister is to-night. He is going to make these people pay to the millers, the men who are producing these goods in Canada, $4 or $5 a ton more than they would pay if he would, by Order in' Council, remove that duty and let them come in free.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Does my hon.
friend not know that it was admitted by the hon. member for Huntingdon (Mr, Robb) that these products are cheaper in Canada to-day than they are in the United States?

All I know is that my hon. friend from Huntingdon wanted to propose an amendment to make these products free and he was ruled out of order, I am afraid, at the instance of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I beg my hon.
friend's pardon. I am sure that he would not wish to make a statement that is entirely incorrect. It never occurred to me that the hon. member for Huntingdon was out of order, nor did I expect to-day, when

I came to the House prepared to discuss the amendment of which I had received notice, that it would be ruled out of order.

I accept that statement from the minister, but that does not alter the fact that my hon. friend from Huntingdon has not had an opportunity yet of presenting his amendment, and anyway I do not think it alters the fact, that wheat products cost more in Canada to-day than they would cost if the duty were removed. If I am not right, if the millers are not making a profit out of the consumers in this country that they ought not to make, if wheat products are not $4 or $5 a ton more than they would be if the duty was removed, why does not the Minister of Finance remove the duty? He could remove the duty on wheat and flour because there was such a demand in the western country that he could not resist it, and I feel satisfied that that political nine-tenths was the thing that removed the duty from wheat and flour. If he could remove the duty from wheat and flour, why could he not go further and remove it from wheat products? The very fact that the minister does not remove that duty, when he has removed the duty from wheat and flour, answers the whole question and answers it in the affirmative, that if the duty were removed the men who use these goods would be getting them cheaper than they are to-day. I do not think it needs any argument because men do these things for reasons.
The next important matteT has been, so ably discussed by my hon. friend from Edmonton that I feel that I would be only uselessly consuming time were I to seek to devote much attention to it. My h,on. friend the Minister of Finance, with his usual sophistry when discussing tariff questions, says: " Why did you not do these things when you were in power; look at what we have done; we have reduced the duties'from 17J per cent down to 12 per cent on mowers, reapers, binders and harvesters." If my hon. friend ever did very much farming he would know that mowers, reapers, binders and harvesters make a very small item in' the list of machinery which the ordinary farmer uses.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not in the West.

Yes, in the West, in the East and all over Canada. I know what I am talking about now because I buy some of this machinery myself. If this was all I had to buy I would not care very much whether there was a duty on at or not. If a

man wants to raise potatoes you have not touched the duty upon the implements that he requires. You are making him pay 20, or 25 per cent on the machinery which he has to buy. Mowing machines and binders are very small things, hut take tractors, manure spreaders, potato planters, cultivators, diggers, sprayers and all those things costing from $75 up 'to $125 and $150, articles which every man in the East must buy if he is going to raise potatoes in a modern way and which will cost from $500 to $700 per farm; the minister has not touched a cent of duty on these and the farmers down East are paying all the way from 174 to 25 per cent on these goods. They are paying that no matter whether they are manufactured in Canada or not because, if they are not manufactured in Canada, they are paying to the revenue, but if they are 'manufactured in Canada they are paying not to the revenue hut to the manufacturers. No matter from what source they come the farmer pays the duty because he has to pay it to somebody. Yet, my hon. friend has not touched this duty. My hon. friend has not touched the big machinery.
He has not touched the thresher; he has not touched the steam threshing outfit; he has not touched anything except three or four of the most ordinary and the cheapest articles which the farmer uses on his farm, unless you count hand forks and rakes, etc. So, after all, I do not think the Minister of Finance can take much credit to himself for having reduced the duty on agricultural implements. There, again, he is trying to get from the farmer a little credit to which he is not entitled. I should like to know by What logic you can say that the dhty should he kept on farm machinery in Canada when you realize that every man who has been in the business, outside of a certain circumscribed territory in the province of Ontario, has absolutely been driven out of existence-and I speak again as a man who knows, as I paid some thousands of dollars in order to see if I could not manufacture a certain kind of farm machinery in competition with the Massey-Harris people, and I failed. I learned to my cost that they could drive me and everybody else out unless he was a man of their substance. I will tell you how they did it. They did not sell much cheaper than I did, but they would give the farmer three years1 time without interest. We could not compete against that, and they drove us out of business, and they have done that with hundreds of people in Canada. We wanted
to manufacture farm machinery and to manufacture it fairly and to sell to our neighbours at a reasonable profit, and, the moment these large concerns drove the smaller man out of business, up went the price and the interest, and to-day, if you buy a thresher down East-and it was threshers that I attempted to manufacture- you pay 7 per cent interest. But when they had some competition down there you could ' get three years' credit without interest. It is all very well for a little clique in a certain portion of Ontario to say: We manufacture farm machinery and we want protection; hut I want to tell you that there are some millions of people who do not live in Ontario, who cannot manufacture farm machinery, and who do not want protection, that is, who do not want a protective duty, but who do want protection from the Government as against these men who are compelling them to pay two prices for machinery. There are a lot of us in Canada in that position.
And then take the trade returns. Last 7 year we imported altogether, of agricul- ) tural implements and parts thereof, everything which you can possibly imagine, ineluding scythes and hand rakes and all / the little things used on the farm, only $1,673,000 worth. I have again 9 p.m. no idea how many million dol- j lars worth are consumed in Canada, but there must be a great many millions, tens of millions of dollars worth of farm machinery consumed and yet we imported only $1,673,000 worth in Canada on which the Government received only $309,000 in duty, a mere bagatelle. And yet, Sir, we paid from 12 per cent to 174 per cent and 25 per cent on all these millions and tens of millions of dollars worth of machinery used in Canada. We paid this, not to the Government, but to a little co-terie^of manufacturers in Ontario, and that . same little coterie of manufacturers in Ontario were able to sell to the rest of the world practically $4,000,000 worth of these same articles. The exact figures are $3,- I
854,000.
Does any man tell me that you must have protection on farm implements in Canada when we are able to sell to the rest of the world from two to three times as much as we import, in addition to manufacturing for our people at home? We sold these goods all over the civilized world ex- , cept in the United States. where the, sales were practically nothing, we sold them in the Argentine Republic, in Australia, in New Zealand, in Britain and in France,

and before the war we sold them in Germany, Austria and Russia. I myself saw Massey Harris machinery in Germany and in France, and at a fair in Ipswich, in England, I saw their machinery for sale cheaper than you could buy it in Canada. I went there and purposely priced the machines to see. They are selling these goods all over the civilized world in competition with the rest of the world, and they can manufacture for home consumption and compete with and under-sell the rest of the world in the foreign markets, and then they will tell you:	We must have protection on these goods; otherwise we will have to close down our 'factory. I was very much interested not long ago in discussing this question with a gentleman on a train. I very seldom talk politics on trains, but I overheard a conversation and finally took a hand in it. Years ago we used to hear the story: Oh, but we can not compete with the rest of the world, we are not in a position to compete with the world; and if you throw down the duty to any appreciable extent, let alone making goods free, we will have to close down our business, we will have to close up our shop and our men will be on the street. There has not been an election in Canada in my day that that argument has not been used, and, I am bound to say, used very effectively in certain parts of Canada. Of course, the whole thing was a farce from the beginning. Nobody believed it excepting the poor labouring man over whose head the bludgeon was held. But now a different idea has come in. These gentlemen realize that this thing will not go any longer. There is no use in the Massey Harris people saying: We can not manufacture in Canada without protection, when it is said that when the war broke out there was $8,000,000 or $10,000,000 owing to them in Germany alone, and when they are able to sell in every part of the world that requires farm implements. They can not say that any longer. But these gentlemen have another story entirely. They say: Yes, it is true that we sell in foreign countries, but we -have to slaughter our goods to sell them there, and if we do not lose money we barely come out alive. But we have to keep our overhead expenses down, and in order to keep these expenses down we are compelled to manufacture in large quantities, and by selling to the home consumer at a good big price and by selling to the outsider at cost or a little 
less, we keep down our overhead expenses and are able to keep our factories going. That is the latest reason I have heard advanced, and a good many times in the last few years. When that is exploded it will be something else.
That brings us back to the main question, why on earth should the Canadian farmer be compelled to pay toll to the man who manufactures his machinery when that same man can supply the home market and compete with every other manufacturer in the world, in the foreign market, successfully? I believe that the Canadian manufacturer is doing a bigger business to-day in many foreign markets than all the rest of the manufacturers of farm machinery in the world combined. That is the real practical question, and that is the question that this House has to decide to-night, so far as that branch of the amendment is concerned. That is a question which I quite understand my hon. friend the Minister of Finance can vote down without any question at all, because he is constituted that way. It really comes natural to him, and I do not think he is violating any principles when he is voting against it. But I want to appeal to some of my farming friends on the other side, some of the men whose constituents are buying these articles; I wonder how they can vote down an amendment of this kind. It may be possible, but it seems to me that they will have to do a good deal of figuring o'n it in order to square this matter with their own consciences, let alone the best interests of the people whom they represent. I want to say again that I am the last man in this House who would by my vote advocate a tariff policy which would drive any man out of business. I do not claim to be a free trader; I do not claim to be a protectionist;
I claim that, in a new country like Canada, it is the proper policy to meet conditions as they exist; and if you find that a certain manufacturer or firm of manufacturers has reached such a point of excellence, if they have made so much money that they can manufacture as cheaply as in any other place in the world, if they can exclude the foreign products from our markets, and are able to and do so manufacture and do so sell that we get no imports and get no revenue from customs duties on these articles, then, Sir, I can see no reason why that concern should be allowed to mulct the common people to the extent they are mulcting them. If you cannot make these articles free, then bring the tariff down as far as you

i
can, so that it will give the manufacturers sufficient protection to enable them to live, but not sufficient protection to enable them to become multi-millionaires at the expense of the common people, who are compelled to-buy their wares. I have no hesitation in saying that the time has come when the duty on farm machinery should be absolutely wiped out. No man need tell me that these people can in ordinary times sell their goods to Britain, Australia, New Zealand, Germany, Austria, Russia and France at less than cost; they are not fools enough to do that. No man need tell me that they are not making bigger profits out of the Canadian consumer than they have any right to make, or than this Parliament is justified in allowing them to make.
What is true of farm implements is true of the rest of the items enumerated in the proposed free list contained in this amendment. I have discussed cement; I wish, for a moment, at the expense of being tiresome, to discuss a matter which is of greater importance to my constituency, to my province and to the province of Quebec than almost anything else in this list, and that 13 fertilizer.
Before the war broke out we were buying the best grade of fertilizer-what we call 4, 8 and 10-; that means 10 per cent potash- at about $40 a ton. On account of the duty the price has gone up. To the credit of my hon. friend, I may say that he did not apply the 7h per cent duty to fertilizers, but a duty of 10 per cent still applies. We cannot successfully grow potatoes without fertilizers. While a few years ago the potato industry was carried on more largely in Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick, to-day the greatest producers of potatoes in Canada are the people on the St. Lawrence river, in the counties of Rimouski, Gaspe, Temis-eouata, Kamouraska, Bonaventure. My hon. friend who sits opposite (Mr. Boulay) will bear out what I say in this respect. Hundreds of thousands of bushels of the finest potatoes in the world are grown in these districts. But to-day we cannot get fertilizer, containing potash; we are compelled to pay $55 a ton for fertilizer without potash. In view of the small revenue the minister gets from this source, he is not justified in compelling the producers of potatoes to pay the present duty upon fertilizers. He talks about production, and more production. He says that the Government have taught the people to produce more; yet he piles up the cost of producing that staple article of food by the imposition
of a duty of 10 per cent, resulting in the farmer being obliged to pay from $5 to $10 more for fertilizers than he would otherwise have to pay. Perhaps I am speaking more warmly on this subject than is becoming, but I know the conditions. I buy the article myself; all my neighbours and constituents have to buy it and I know that they cannot produce without it. Yet we are told to produce more. When I was home last week, the great cry of the people was: we cannot get fertilizer on account of the enormous price which the minister makes us pay for it. The removal of that duty would be a great benefit to the people of Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick, and Quebec. If for no other reason, therefore, I am compelled to support this amendment because of the vital importance of this matter to my province.
Another principle which is set forth in this resolution is dear to my heart. I shall not call it trade for trade, as my hon. friend did this afternoon; I shall call it reciprocity. When the House met after the election of 1911 it was stated by some hon. gentlemen opposite that reciprocity was dead. J said (that reciprocity was just as much alive as ever. Call it reciprocity, trade for trade, or what you will; the principle involved in reciprocity was good in 1911, and it is better to-day. The Minister of Finance has admitted that he has gone back on every word that he uttered on reciprocity. He has eaten crow with the best face of any man that I ever saw in my life, and he smacked his lips over it. He said, I know I was wrong in what I said in 1911; nothing is so good for this country tas free wheat. And he has admitted that the member fpr SB Antoine (Sir Herbert Ames) was wrong when he said that if wheat be made free, the very cornerstone of our trade is removed. The member foT St. Antoine a few weeks ago, meek as a little boy, said: free wheat is all right; we have to take it; it is a good thing. These hon. gentlemen, by advocating the adoption of free -fliheat, have said in effect that reciprocity is good in 1917 and that it was good in 1911. Millions of people in Canada say that reciprocity is right. In this amendment is embodied the principle that food and food products, animals and the foods therefor, should be admitted into Canada free of duty from any country which makes similar tariff provisions. Some gentlemen contended six years ago that if this policy were adopted, you would not be able to sell cattle. I dp not

know whether I could tell you what some gentlemen argued in the We-st at that time- they told so many different stories in different parts of the country-but one thing they said in New Brunswick was that if we had reciprocity, the Yankees would come over and steal our lumber. They are ' coming over now and paying $35 -a thousand for out lumber, which we used to sell at $12 and $14. Of course, I do not say that that is entirely because the duty has been taken off lumber, but a large part of the result may be attributed to that cause. We have secured a certain amount of reciprocity by the removal of duties by the United States. I am going to watch some of my good Conservative friends with a great deal of interest so that I may see the wry faces they will make if the Americans put back the duty of 10 per cent on many of the articles going into their country from Canada. You will find out then whether hon. gentlemen opposite believe in reciprocity or not. It will also be a matter of interest and curiosity to me-possibly I may be animated by another feeling-to watch some of my good friends and see how they take the imposition of say $6 or $7 on a two year old steer, $3 on a thousand feet of lumber, and various amounts on other things now going to the United States and for which we are receiving magnificent prices. I am glad, Sir, that my hon. friend has included this principle in his amendment. I repeat that the principle is just as good to-day as it was in 1911. The items mentioned in the amendment are just as deserving of consideration as was free wheat. Free wheat is good for the farmer of the West. It is good for the farmer of the East, because it gives him cheaper bread, but free wheat does not mean so much to him as the removal -of the duty on some of the items included in this amendment would mean.
The fourth paragraph of the amendment provides for a general reduction of tariff on all artiles imported into Canada except luxuries. Wiih that principle I heartily agree. But one article which, in my judgment, has ceased to be a luxury-which, as a matter of fact, has become a real necessity to the farming community-is the automobile.
I realize that down to a very recent date automobiles were a luxury; and while I think a duty of 42J per cent is outrageous, still there is no doubt there was a time when that duty was justifiable. The time, however, has now come when in the West and in the East and in all the farming

communities of Canada, the people not only want the automobile for the pleasure of the thing, but really demand it and regard it as a necessity on the farms. Probably nothing has made farm life in Canada as pleasant and attractive as has the automobile and also, the rural telephone, and I know of no greater pleasure than to see a farmer, after he has done his day's work, take his wife to town in his car and perhaps go to a picture show or a theatre and return home by ten o'clock. The automobile has become a necessity for a farmer taking trips into town for repairs for his machinery and for a hundred and one things that are required around a farm. When one realizes that an automobile which costs $1,000 in the state of Maine, ten miles from my home, would cost $1,425 on this side of the line, one can hardly credit it. I can go ten miles from my home and buy a car for four or five or six hundred dollars less than I can buy it in my own town. I would not mind paying a reasonable duty on an automobile because I know that we must raise a revenue, hut why an automobile should be worth $100 more on this side of the Detroit river than on the other is something that I can not understand, and why on earth a better class of car costs $200 more in my town than in the town of Houlton in the United States ten miles away, is, something also that I cannot understand. There is another thing that makes the tax even more burdensome. This old story about infant industries is becoming practically exhausted in Canada. Up to a few years ago, one heard it said: You must encourage the infant industries. But some of those infants have stuck to the bottle for many years, and some of them will die upon the bottle, let alone live on it. I find, as regards the automobile industry, that not only do we manufacture a very large percentage of the automobiles which we use in Canada, but last year we exported $9,431,000 worth of automobiles' and we shipped them to all parts of the world. When I first saw those figures I thought they referred to motor trucks and cars of that kind that were sent over to Great Britain on account of this war. That is not the case. A very small proportion went to Great Britain, but we shipped automobiles to the Argentine, Australia, New Zealand, Newfoundland, the West Indies, and other countries. Therefore, we are able to manufacture automobiles, not only for our own market, hut to compete

with the rest of the world, and yet you tell me you require a duty of 421 per cent to-day iff order to keep a few little automobile factories running in Canada. The Ford factory is the only one in Canada that is making automobiles; the Other so-called automobile factories are only assembling the parts which are imported from the United States. I will admit that they manufacture a few bodies, but outside of factories manufacturing bodies and assembling parts, I know of no concern in Canada except the Ford which manufactures automobiles. There was one in Toronto, but it was sold out to an American firm which is now using that plant only for assembling parts. It is true that the parts that are imported are subject to a duty of 42i per cent, but in the whole realm of commerce there is no article that is more susceptible of manipulation than an automobile part. Take, for example, the rear axle containing the differential. You take an ordinary $1,000 or $1,200 car, and you want to bring in that axle, and the factory will charge you $125 for it, but they will bring it in as a casting, and it will cost them only $15 and they will pay the duty on the value of that article as a casting. They bring these parts in at a nominal figure, and they pay duty only on that figure; they assemble the parts in this country and they sell them to*our farmers adding 42J per cent on the total value. For instance, they might pay $100 in duty on the parts of an automobile that they assemble, and they will charge the people $400 for doing so. That is a matter which comes as near to me as anything in the whole realm of commerce, and it is something which I am, in the most serious possible manner, calling to the attention of the Minister of Finance. It is true we get some revenue on importations of automobiles, but we shall get a good deal more revenue if you will cut the duty in half or even cut it down to a third, because in that case you will find that the people will import more automobiles. The farmer on the western prairie who cannot afford to buy a car now will be able to have one then, and a man down East who has saved up $500 or $600 and who says that he cannot afford to pay $1,000 for an automobile will be able to buy one. In that way, more automobiles will be imported and the Government will get as much revenue out of those importations as they will under present conditions, but the man or the American company who has a factory over in Canada assembling automobiles will not make as much money out of the business as he is making out of the people of Canada to-day. There is no doubt about that. As far as I am concerned-and I think I am voicing the sentiment of every man in this House, no matter on which side he sits-I am sure we would all like to see the ordinary farmer, and even the labouring man, if you will, be in a position to buy an automobile, rather than to see the dollars piled up in the pockets of the American manufacturer who assembles parts in the Dominion of Canada.
The last item of this amendment refers to the British preference, and I know there is nothing in the whole list which is so distasteful to the Minister of Finance as is the proposal to increase the British preference.
I do not think my hon. friend feels that way towards it because he has any real objection to trading with Great Britain. I am not charging him with anything like that; I never charge any one with die-loyalty, because I think the meanest thing on earth is for one Canadian to say to another: You are disloyal. I am not intimating that for one moment. The minister knows that there is no greater blow to high protection in Canada than the British preference. He knows that the British preference works out, not in one way, but in three ways. He knows that if you increase the British preference to 50 per cent, then any article which can be brought into Canada from Great Britain or any of the Dominions that have the same arrangement, will come in by paying half the duty which the same article will pay if imported from a foreign country, and if the matter would stop there, the minister would not feel so badly about it; but he knows there are two other phases to this question. He knows that if the foreigner wants to bring that same article into Canada he must sell it at a price which, with the duty added, will not make the cost to the consumer any more than the British article will cost with one-half the duty added, and he knows that he will probably derive less revenue unless he has a bigger importation. There is, however, a third phase of the question which is still more important to my hon. friend and to Canada, and that is that the home manufacturer must sell his goods at a price low enough to compete with the article which comes from Great Britain, with one-half Oif the duty chargeable against it, or with the foreign article cut down in price so as to meet the British preference. Therefore,

every time you increase the British preference on an article you make that article cheaper, whether it comes from Great Britain or from a foreign country or if it is manufactured in Canada. You will find you are not only making it cheaper to the consumer, but you are stimulating importations, because if it is cheaper, people will be able to buy more of it; more of it will be imported and the result will be at the end of the year you will have just as much revenue with the British preference increased to 50 per cent as you have now with the British preference around 33 per cent.
I have gone over the paragraphs of this amendment a little more in detail perhaps than was necessary, but it is a very important matter to me. I do not want to leave this subject before trying to answer in a very hurried way the question which my hon. friend put this afternoon, and I knew it was coming, /because It'he very moment you talk about reducing the tariff hon. gentlemen opposite ask:	Where are
you going to get the revenue? I tried to take down the minister's exact words this afternoon. He said: "We could not raise the money without the tariff; it is and must be the main source of revenue." He said the tariff could not be revised in war time, and that we could not get along without it. I have not asked him to do without the tariff. I have never asked and never will ask a government to remove the tariff on any article if by so doing they would prevent the article being manufactured in Canada under ordinary conditions. But I say and shall continue to say until common sense methods prevail with the government of this country that when an article is manufactured so cheaply in Canada as to prevent the importation of the foreign article, that article requires no protection; it is paying no duty, and it requires no protection. In the case of such articles I ask the Government to remove the duty entirely, so as to allow the people to get the benefit of the amount of money they are now paying to the Canadian manufacturer. When I find that the duty on an article makes the people of this country pay more than they should for their boots and shoes and many other items I might mention, then I say it is the duty of the Government to cut that duty down to such a point that the people will not be compelled to pay an jexhorbitant price, and the country will get some revenue by the importation of the foreign article.
I have already pointed out jhat in the case of boots and shoes the duty 
amounts to less than three-quarters of a million dollars, including the 7i per cent. I would cut the duty down so that the people would have the choice of bringing the article in at a fair price or of buying from Ames, Holden & McCready at a fair price. I would put those people where they could not sell their watered stock for good money and they say later on: You must not touch the duty on these goods or you will render valueless the stock for which good money has been paid. And similarly with regard to cement and many other items, such as farm machinery and automobiles to quite an extent. My hon. friend will say: We must have these duties in war time, because we cannot raise money in any other way. I do not think my hon. friend does himself justice when he makes t'he statement that he cannot raise revenue except by the customs tariff. My hon. friend has a pretty good opinion of himself as a financier, and I admit that he knows quite a lot about finance; he understands the question pretty well.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not any too well.

Fairly well. He knows more about it than I do, if that is any consolation to him, and I cannot understand why a man who knows as much about finance as he does, who can keep the finances of this country in a better condition than the finances of any other country in the world except the United States, cannot find some other method of raising the revenue except by customs tariff. My hon. friend has found out something:	He has
taxed the business interests of Canada. He has taxed the banks. My! but he hit them a gentle blow, one of those beautiful love-taps that my hon. friend reserves for the big interests. He has learned how to tax the common people on every letter they send across the seas. He knows how to do all these things, and now he comes and says, I can do no more, I am done.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, no.

My hon. friend is taking all these taxes out of the common people anyhow, and no matter whether he has to raise $230,000,000 or $330,000,000 in the future he realizes that it has to come out of the pockets of the people of Canada in some way or other, and does he mean to tell me that with all his knowledge of finance he knows of no way of raising the revenue except by custom duties? Never for a moment.
He is too modest.

He is not as modest as all that. I will not go over the question of an income tax, as we have discussed that time and again in this House. I will not discuss the land tax, though personally I believe there is no tax in the world that is so equitable and just. They tried the experiment in the province of Ontario last year, imposing only a small tax,about 2 mills I think-it was a nominal sum any way-and they got more money than they knew what to do with. I am sure that the Minister of Finance by imposing a moderate land tax could raise half the revenue he now raises from the whole Dominion. But he only wants a tariff revenue, and he says that he knows of no other method. I can tell him that there will be some man in his seat before very long who will know what to do, and how to do it, and just as soon as the people of this country get a chance they will show him what to do. I want to tell him that all is not well in Canada, notwithstanding the very 'glowing statement he made this afternoon. Go and talk to the labouring man in the towns and villages in any part of Canada. I grant you that he is getting more money than he ever did before, perhaps $2.50 a day, Or if he is a munitions worker from $3 to $5 a day. But go into that man's home and ask him what he thinks of present conditions. You will find that he has to pay.$7 or $8 for a pair of boots for his wife which formerly cost him only $3.50 and $16 a barrel for flour and 13 and 14 cents for a loaf that used to cost him 10 cents. He cannpt buy woollens at all, because the price has gone up out of sight, and my hon. friend has imposed a tarifi of 35 or 40 per cent. Every trticle pf food and clothing that the poor man uses in his home has been multiplied in price until he does not know how to make ends meet. The common people of this country are thinking deeply about these matters. To the ordinary labouring man or the clerk in the store, the man working for a daily wage or for a small salary, the problem of the cost of living is becoming-I was going to say almost a greater problem than the war itself, and it is men of this class who are winning the war; it is not the plutocrats who have shed their blood and spent their money to win this war. I:t is the common everyday people, the labouring man and the farmers' sons who have volunteered and gone to the front, and the question which is agitating the common people of this country to-day is the high cost of living. Wherever three or four women are gathered together, whether they be rich or
poor, high or low, after discussing the latest hats you will always find them talking about the cost of living. The question is in everybody's mouth; the problem is with every man who has to earn a living for himself and family. No matter how my hon. friend may draw his cloak around this question, no matter what sophistries his monopolistic friends may preach to him, I : can tell him that the common people are i thinking of this question as they never i thought of anything before since 'Canada \ was Canada, and the people will find a way if my hon. friend cannpt; they will find a way, and they will find the man to get rid of this burden on the necessities of life. They will show my hon. friend how to raise the revenue, and 'how to make the man who has grown rich out of tariffs and out ,of the present war pay his fair share into the treasury of this country, not only while the war is on but after the war, when I believe terrible conditions will exist and additional taxation will have to be raised.

I understand the argument of the hon. member for Carleton, N.B. (Mr. Carvell) to be that duties have very much effect upon the prices of goods. I desire * to call his attention to several items with which I am familiar. * First, I take agricultural implements-I speak particularly of the mowers and binders used in the west. The reduction of duty that has been made in agricultural implements has been made almost wholly by the Conservative Government. The duty was at first 35 per cent. A Conservative Government reduced it to 20 per cent. The succeeding Liberal Government reduced this duty to 171 per cent, and under the Conservative Government it has been cut down to 121 per cent. Yet we are paying more for agricultural implements to-day than we paid when the duty was 171 per cent. Take the case of flour. The duty on this article has been removed altogether. We are paying more for flour than we did when a duty was charged. The hon. gentlemen referred also to boots. The duty under the Conservative Government was 25 per cent. Our friends on the other side, though they talk so much of low tariff, increased that duty to 30 per cent. I did not rise for the purpose of making any extensive remarks, but I wished to call the attention of the hon. gentleman to these facts, which he cannot dispute.

Why did not you ask
the hon. member for St. Antoine (Sir Herbert Ames) to make that statement.

I make my own statements without reference to any other man. It happens that the hon. member for St. Antoine sits beside me, but that has nothing to do with the matter. The question is, are these facts or are they not?
Is the hon. gentleman asking a question or making a statement?
I was correcting the hon. gentleman's error.
Then he does not expect any reply from me.

No resolution has 'come before this House which it has given me greater pleasure to support than this amendment proposed by the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver). The reduction of the tariff is an idea very dear to the hearts of the people of that part of the country which I represent, and for that reason as well as because it commends itself to my own judgment, I strongly support this amendment. The Minister of Finance this afternoon took great credit to the Government for the raising of 400,000 men and sending them overseas to take part in the war. From my knowledge of the methods of recruiting and equipping the Canadian army, I take exception to the hon. minister's statement. I come from a city which, I believe, has done more for recruiting, according to its population, than any other in t(he Dominion, and I think the same applies to the province of Alberta as a whole. I say that our success in raising a large number of men for the front was not owing to any action taken by this Government, but to the extremely patriotic feeling which pervaded all classes of the people. When the war broke out no government could have stopped the men in my province from volunteering and enlisting; in fact, when it was first known that war was on, the difficulty was to prevent- men from going. I venture to say that if the Department of Militia had used business-like methods in recruiting the first contingent, and, later on, the rest of the men required for overseas service we should not to-day be confronted with the problem of conscription.
The Minister of Finance also took a great deal of credit to the Government for the way in which the Canadian war loans have been subscribed. I admit that these domestic loans were a new departure in finance, and the minister is entitled to credit for his acumen in resorting to them. But he must not overlook the fact that there is no in-
vestment in Canada which offers equal security and equal return on investment with exemption from war taxation. It would be poor business on the part of any man or woman in Canada who has money to invest not to buy a bond or more as their circumstances permit.
I was much disappointed when the Budget was brought down to find that no tariff changes were made. We are confronted with the terrible difficulty of providing foodstuffs for the Allies in spite of obstacles to transportation. We are urged on all sides to increase production and to do everything	to	enable the Allies to
feed and care for the men at the front. In my province, where agriculture is a basic industry, and where conditions are	excellently suited for
the raising of all kinds of grain, one of the first problems confronting our farmers is the duty on agricultural implements. We believe that the western prairie provinces are bound to be the greatest grain-producing section in the whole Dominion. We believe, therefore, that it is absolutely essential that everything should be done that can be done to make production there as economical and as efficient as possible. For that reason I am strongly in favour of the amendment, which declares for the reduction of taxes on implements required for use on the farm. A commission has been appointed to investigate the high cost of living, and to learn what can be done to ameliorate the conditions under which the masses of the people are struggling at this time. We have also had a discussion in this House within the past few days as to price agreements which are to-day in effect as between the manufacturers and wholesale dealers. I understand that this commission, appointed by the Minister of Labour, has been investigating these matters from coast to coast, and that they have in their possession copies of such price agreements as were brought to the attention of the Ho'use by the hon. member for Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles) a few nights ago. And yet we are not informed that any action has been taken by the Government, or even by the Minister of Labour, to bring the parties to these agreements to time, and thus to effect a saving in the cost of the necessaries of life for the people. The combines between manufacturers and wholesalers have been in existence for a great many years.
One particular combine which I have seen in my province is the sugar combine. The sugar refining industry is in the hands practically of three or four firms in Canada.

The British Columbia Refining Company operate from Vancouver east as far as Brandon. From there the eastern manufacturers control the price and it is a straight combine price in every city and town between Vancouver and Montreal. The question of value apparently does not enter into the computation at all. Sugar is sold cheaper in Brandon than in Regina and yet it may be supplied from Vancouver. Sugar is sold cheaper in Yorkton than in Edmonton and yet the distance from the shipping point is from 300 to 500 miles greater in the former case than in the latter. The same thing applies with respect to a great many other lines of stable goods which are absolutely required by the people of this country. Yet, the commission which was supposed to deal with questions of this kind and to find a solution, if possible, has done nothing to alleviate conditions and to-day we are confronted with a terrible rise in prices of all food commodities. Prices have gone on increasing until we have reached a stage where it is practically impossible for people to live with any degree of comfort.
Another question in regard to which the Government has 'been derelict in its duty is that of supplying seed to the farmers for the increased production which hon. gentlemen opposite have been advocating. The cultivation of potatoes is a matter of very great importance to the country at the present time. I suppose there is no food product which is in more common use and which is of greater importance to the people of any country than the potato and the importance of a plentiful supply of this commodity is obvious to every one. The Government, through their Minister of Agriculture, or through the commission appointed to investigate the high cost of living, must have known that the supply of seed potatoes was very scarce and that the price was skyrocketing. Yet the Minister of Agriculture did nothing outside of making a few inquiries in the different' provinces as to the number of bushels of potatoes which were available. The result of this inquiry must have shown him that the situation was extremely serious inasmuch as he was informed that only in three provinces had they a surplus. He took steps to provide seed wheat, oats and barley to the farmers of eastern Canada and yet he neglected to arrange for a supply of seed potatoes which his department could have secured fcr the farmers of Ontario,
Quebec and other provinces who required that seed. The result of that policy of inaction is that to-day -when planting is on, a large acreage which otherwise would have been planted with potatoes will go without the necessary seed being put in to ensure a satisfactory crop to our own people. Any one planting potatoes has to pay such an exorbitant price for the seed that it is very questionable, even if he has a good crop, whether he will get a sufficient return in the fall for the cost of the seed and his labour.
Last year a duty was added to a food necessity of the western provinces particularly which is obtained from British Columbia and the western states. I refer to apples. Apples have become a necessity of the prairie provinces. We are not able to grow them ourselves and it is absolutely essential that we should import them. This Government in its wisdom, last year, raised the duty on. apples until to-day the duty is 90 cents a barrel. This was done at the request of the growers in British Columbia. I think that is a fair statement. I do not think that any growers in eastern Canada particularly urged upon the Government that this duty should be increased. We, in western Canada at least, thought that we were being mulcted for the benefit of the fruit growers of British Columbia. The result of that duty has teen this: We were told at the time that the duty was put on that we would get as good a grade of fruit as we had been getting, that we would pay no more for apples, that the British Columbia growers would be able to produce and ship at a profit, and we would be en-cpuraging industry in our own country and not doing ourselves any harm. What has been the result? I have lived in western Canada for twenty-two years and I have never yet seen as poor a quality of apples put on the market in Alberta as we had this year and we have never paid as high a price. The argument may be put forth that the apple crop was a failure in Ontario last year and that that was the reason why our apples were higher in the West. As a matter of fact, we do not bring apples from eastern Canada farther west than Regina or Moosejaw. The apples consumed in Alberta come from British Columbia or from Oregon. In spite of the fact that a duty of 90 cents per barrel was put on apples, importers were compelled to buy from Oregon and Washington quite a large quantity on which a considerable duty was paid. In answer to a question I put on the

Order Paper I was informed that the total amount of duty collected from the importation of green apples imported into Canada from the United States during the fiscal year ended March 1917, was $250,155.90. That was the import duty on apples coming in from the United States. I also asked what was the total amount of duty collected on green apples imported into Canada from the United States at the ports of Calgary and Edmonton respectively during the year *ending March, 1917, and I find that in Calgary we paid duty to the amount of $17,373.60 and in Edmonton to the amount of $20,038.90. When this duty of 90 cents a barrel was put on it was generally stated, by gentlemen representing British Columbia constituencies, that it was not a duty for revenue. It was absolutely a protective duty imposed explicitly for the purpose of shutting out American apples from Canada, yet, in spite of that fact, we in western Canada, in the two ports of Calgary and Edmonton, were forced to pay duty on American apples from the state of Washington and the state of Oregon to the extent of nearly $40,000, protecting the whole British Columbia crop to the extent of 90 cents a barrel. The way in which we were served was that we received the poorest stuff. The grading was the poorest it has ever been in my experience, and I question very much if the British Columbia grower is much better off than he was a year ago before that additional duty was put on. If the Minister of Agriculture were in his place I would call his attention to the way in which his inspectors have been marking and classifying apples under the pure food laws. The grading of apples coming in from the American side, I was told by importers who had no object in telling me this that except that it was the absolute truth, is entirely unsatisfactory; I am told that no matter what the grade of apples coming in from the other side might be, the inspector on the Canadian side marked the fruit number two. It is well known that the grading of apples on the American side in the Western States is higher in standard than on the Canadian side, and the object of marking all the stock number two is something that I do not understand.
Upon the amendment introduced by the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), I want to make a few remarks, even at the risk of repeating many of the arguments that have been so ably advanced by the hon. member for Edmonton and the hon. member for Carleton, N. B. (Mr. Carvell).

The subject is so dear to my heart, that I feel it my duty to discuss this question, even at the risk of such repetition. The first clause is that wheat, wheat flour and other products of wheat be placed upon the free list. This policy has been adopted by the present Government to a large extent, with the exception of bran, shorts, middlings and other products of wheat. The principle has been accepted by the Government, so that in asking that this clause be enlarged to include bran, shorts, middlings and other products of wheat, we are not asking anything which should not be granted if the Government are sincere in.placing these art-
10 p.m. icles of wheat, wheat flour and semolina on the free list by Order in Council a few weeks ago.
The second clause relates to farm implements and machinery and farm tractors. I have gone into the amount of duty which we have collected on the different lines of farm machinery during the .year 1915-16, the last period for which returns are available, and I find that on nearly all the lines of farm implements that might be used ,on a western farm, including binders, cultivators, drills, rollers, harrows, hay loaders, hay tedders, horserakes, manure spreaders, threshing machines, ploughs, reapers, mowing machines and parts thereof, other agricultural implements and parts thereof, the total amount of duty collected was $446,111.-49-less than half a million dollars collected on all those different items of farm machinery, articles which have got to be used by every farmer, not only in western Canada but also in eastern Canada, on which he is mulcted to the amount of that duty, no matter whether it is 12i per cent or 25 per cent, although we are toeing urged, not only by the Canadian Government but by the Imperial Government as well, to conduct a policy of production, and yet more production, nothing is done on the part of the Government to assist the farmer in any way or to induce him to cultivate more land. It is well known that a farmer cannot bring additional land under cultivation in a day, or a week, or six months; if he is a business man, he must look ahead and see that he will have a market for his produce, that if he breaks up or acquires additional land and puts it under cultivation the transaction will be a profitable one to him, and that it will be to his advantage to raise more cattle, sheep, grain or whatever he is producing. If the Government had heen anxious to assist in procuring more production, the removal of the duty on farm im-

plements would have been a great assistance. It is what the farmers have insistently ashed for for many years, and it would have had more effect in .stimulating production than almost anything else that I know of. In relation to farm tractors, it is difficult to ascertain the exact amount of duty paid. These tractors are included in the customs returns with large and heavy tractors and it is almost impossible to find out the duty collected on these particular items whidh would be affected by this resolution.
As for flour-and saw-milling machinery, the amount of duty collected on these items is not very great, and if we place lumber and flour on the free list, it is only fair that the machinery which is used in the producing of these articles should also be placed on the free list. The amount of duty collected on sawmilling machinery for 1915-16 was only $36,825.27. The amount of duty on mining machinery, much of which is already free, including ore crushers, with which -are included rock crushers (which are not properly mining machinery) -was $90,587.
In going over the entire list, I find that on coal oil, kerosene oil, the amount of duty collected in 1915-16 was $160,534.41; and on the products of petroleum, which would include lubricating and fuel oil, another $155,993.63, which makes a total duty collected of $316,528.04. When you consider that practically every one in Canada occupying a position in the rural life of the country and every labouring man in many parts of the cities of Canada is a user of kerosene oil, it is surprising to find that we are forced to pay to a combine a duty of two and one-half cents a gallon, the Government receives only $316,000 from that -source of revenue. While the duty of 2J cents does not seem to be very high, on an ad valorem basis it means a protection of 45 per cent or over. This is a tariff not for revenue, but absolutely for protection. It is put on for the purpose of preventing the importation of oil, and it has the effect of enhancing the price to every user of oil in Canada.
What is the duty on the raw product?

The raw product is free, with the exception of 7J per cent war tax. The hon. member for Carleton has gone into the question of cement, showing that we received less than $10,000 during the year 1915-16 from the duty on that article.
From the duty on fertilizers we received $59,986.25. I have given the amounts received during the year 1915-16 by way of duty upon the items included in the second section of the - amendment -submitted by the hon. member for Edmonton, the total of which amounted to $959,418.74. It would not unduly press upon the revenues of Canada to give relief to a large number of people and to aid production by the removal of these duties, (because the revenue would -be affected only to the extent of less than a million dollars.
The next principle set forth in the reso- . lution is:
That staple foods and food products, other than wheat and flour, domestic animals and foods therefor, be admitted into Canada free of duty when coming from and being the product of any country admitting like Canadian articles into such country free of duty.
This is the principle which was advocated in 1911 in the reciprocity pact. I was firmly convinced,at that time that the principle was correct, -sound and logical, and I have since had no reason to change my mind.
That substantial reduction be made in tbe general tariff on all articles imported into Canada except luxuries is another principle which we, as Liberals, stand for. I hope that the Government will, by adopting the amendment, carry that principle into effect.
I was able to observe some of the benefits of the British preference when it was first introduced in 1897. I was engaged in business at that time, -and I saw the practical workings of tbe reduction of a straight 33 1-3 per cent in the- duties upon all articles imported into Canada from Great Britain. From the consumer's standpoint, no -act of any Canadian Government was ever of greater value than the putting into efieet of the British preference in 1897. We were enabled to import manufactured goods of good quality -at reasonable prices, giving to the consumers an opportunity of obtaining the finest line o-f cotton and woollen goods ever brought into the country. We were able to give more trade to the Mother Country than we have ever given since; our present trade returns with the United States show that that is the -case. When the Liberal Government changed the British preference of 1897 they made a great mistake.
If they had left the preference at a straight 33 1-3 per cent the consumers of Canada would have derived from it an untold benefit. I want to see that preference re-established and enlarged so that we shall be able to purchase cotton and woollens from the



country which leads the world in the manufacture of those articles. While certain lines of manufactured goods in Canada would be adversely affected, we must not forget that the large body o* consumers must be taken care of or they will not stay in the country.
I should like to make a few suggestions as to how the Government might raise the amount of money which would be taken away by putting on the free list the articles enumerated in this amendment. I am living in a part of the country which has a tremendous amount of unimproved farm lands. I am quite in accord with the view expressed by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Cruise) that the Government would be well advised in putting a direct tax on all unimproved lands in Canada. I have not gone into the figures as carefully as the member for Dauphin with regard to the amount which could be derived.from such a tax, but I am convinced that it would be substantial, more than enough to compensate any change made in the tariff to alleviate the condition of the working people.
I would advocate, also, a graduated income tax. I would exempt incomes of $2,000 and less, for a man who earns $2,000 a year is not earning any too much. The tax on incomes exceeding that amount would, if properly looked after by the Minister of Finance and his department, result in the raising of a very large revenue. He has imposed a graduated tax on corporations and firms; I do not know that I would go any further than he has gone along that line. He is probably looking into the question carefully, and is, perhaps, getting as much money from that source as he can get.
As to the question of free wheat, I would urge the Government, if they do not accept the amendment of the member for Edmonton, to make the measure providing for free wheat a permanent tariff change. In the growing of wheat it is absolutely essential that the producer shall have some guarantee that his market will not be interfered with by the mere whim of any ministry which may be in power.	'
If he wishes to ensure permanency and stability on the part of the grain grower in western Canada, he can do that in no safer and better way than by enacting the legislation which he has brought into force by Order in Council so as to make free wheat a permanent item in the tariff law. I would also urge upon him the necessity of putting oats, barley and flax on the same level as he has put wheat. If he will grant these requests, he may even get a few

votes from his Conservative friends who otherwise might vote with the Opposition.

Mr. Speaker, I feel that I would be failing in my duty to my constituents if I did not support this amendment, as I, amongst others, received in 1911 a mandate from the people to support a policy along the same lines, and this mandate has not yet expired. This amendment, however, goes somewhat further than the reciprocity proposal, and I only wish that at that time the reciprocity proposal had gone as far, because although it was defeated, it would have suited me a great deal better had its scope been wider, as I have always felt that the development, not only of the West but of the whole of Canada, which it is always claimed depends upon the development of the West, depends on freedom of trade -with the United States to a large extent. We, however, failed to obtain a majority in 1911, and vve have been fighting for freedom of trade with the United States ever since. The hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) has now brought the matter up again. There are, in his amendment, one or two features which are not exactly as I would like them to be, and I will refer to them later. I would have been pleased had the amendment gone a little farther. The Minister of Finance -stated to-day that this is a bad time to revise the tariff, but -some hon. members have pointed out that the tariff has already been revised, although in an upward direction, with the exception of wheat, wheat flour and .semolina. Why the Minister of Finance or the Government did, as the hon. member for Carleton stated, " eat crow " in this respect, I do not know. Some reasons have been given, one of them being that the United States are now our allies, which they were not before, and that we must pool our wheat with them. If that is good with regard to wheat and flour, it must hold good with regard to other food products.
But so far as wheat is concerned, wheat for export was always free, that is, it could be shipped through in bond and milled either in the United States, or in the old country, but under this Order in Council, we now have that great American market and we appreciate it very much, no -matter what the motive may be. It is just possible for us to . feel that the motive might not have been along the lines of the reasons given, and it is not an illegitimate conclusion to come to that there were other influences at work. The Financial Post, on April 28, 1917, says:

Further consideration of the free wheat legislation brings the conviction that it represents a change of policy brought about not so much by war conditions as by the influence of that growing force in Western Canada to which reference has several times been made in these columns. The recent tour of Hon. Arthur Meighen probably did more than anything else to open the eyes of the Government as to the importance of meeting the Grain Growers' demands.
In another article the Financial Post makes the statement:
Over all prevails the impression that western Canada is a growing force in politics.
Whatever the motive may have been, we are very glad to have wheat on the free list, but we would like to see a good many other things on the free list. In this regard we are not asking for a special favour; we are asking that our protection be taken away from us; we do not want it; we do not ask for it. We say: Remove the obstacle from our path; if we have anything to sell, allow us to sell it, and do not throw obstacles in the way that will prevent us from selling it. If it is important that the best market be obtained for manufactured products, why is it not important that the best market be obtained for natural products? Let us find the man who wants to buy our food products, and let us endeavor to get them'as rapidly as possible to this man, whoever or wherever he may be. We do not ask for any favour; we simply want the privileges that are unjust to be taken away from those who have no right to them. We do not ask this as class legislation. The West is a new country; we have what was once Rup'ert's Land attached to Canada and it is now considered that it will become the most important part of Canada; but while it has millions of acres of fertile land which should be productive, that land will never produce as it should until some inducement is given to the people to go on the land and until they are made to realize that they can do so profitably. A man who has a family and responsibilities is entitled, when he engages in a life occupation, to some reward if he can secure it legitimately. It is all very well to say to a man: Go to the West and go on the land, but you must show him that he can make a permanent home there, make a living, bring up his family properly and become a good citizen. I would like to read a couple of extracts with regard to this question: In the Forest Free Press of February 1, I find this, referring to the appeal made by the Minister of Agriculture for production and more production:
In the tremendous strain yet to come a vital factor will be an ample and unfailing flow of *0. England and France. No matter what difficulties may face us, the supreme duty of every man on the land is to use every energy in the direction of producing more, and still more.
Now, we hold the same view. * The Government apparently does not. but at the same time they are appealing for more and more production. I have another quotation here along the same lines:
In the three last fiscal years the duty paid on imported farm implements was over six million dollars, while the taxes on home-manufactured implements was over twenty million. In the same three years Canadian manufacturers exported seventeen million dollars worth of farm implements. During these same three years the manufactures were refunded over five million dollars of the duty they had paid on their raw material. Of this amount nearly two million went in aid of the manufacturers of farm machinery and tools sold at home or abroad. The last official census shows that the total value of farm products in that year only 15 per cent on the capital invested, while the product value of farm implements manufactured was 46 per cent, on capital invested.
Under this odious and discriminating policy agriculture has become so unprofitable and has languished to such an extent that the Dominion and Provincial Governments are spending this year some two million dollars, (mostly contributed by the farmers themselves), in frantic appeals to the farmers to produce more food stuffs. The Barons are very much interested in keeping up production, for several good reasons-the Railway Barons enrich themselves in carrying those products at extortionate rates; the Implement Barons want the home market kept up, while both want the farmer to continue to pay their taxes as well as his own.
And it concludes by showing that Ontario is affected as well as the West. Mr. J. H. Pettypiece says:
The great need in this connection is the removal of every vestige of the fiscal taxation which is depopulating our Ontario farms.
That surely is not in the interests of production. It is the opinion of one who is particularly well qualified to speak on this subject. One of the worst features in connection with the tariff is that it allows the establishment of combines. There is a law against combines, I believe, but the only case that was ever proceeded with that I know of was some years ago against a lumber company at Edmonton. Combines have continued to flourish notwithstanding and to a considerable extent they are the cause of the high cost of ^living, and they can only exist. and take shelter behind a protective tariff. I have here the opinion of Alexander Macdonald, head of the A. Macdonald Company, wholesale grocers, Winnipeg:
109i

I am surprised at the statement in the Free Press, attributed to Mr. Carpenter, local secretary of The -Canadian Manufacturers' Association, in which he says that he does not know of a single instance where any manufacturer dictates what price the retailer shall sell to the consumer for. This seems strange, particularly, coming from a gentleman in ^Ir. Carpenter's position, who should be, but is evidently not, conversant with the facts of his office.
The Shredded Wheat Company, an American concern with a Canadian factory, not only dictates what the wholesaler shall sell shredded wheat at, but they stipulate what price the retailer shall charge the consumer, and if he does not adhere to their dictated price, they notify all wholesale jobbers that they are not to supply said retailer with shredded wheat, or if they do, they cannot procure any more shredded wheat from them. The margin of profit in this case is 40 per cent between the price paid by the jobber and what the consumer has to pay.
Then the Edwardsburg Starch Co., and the Borden Milk Co., of New York, which controls certain milk canning factories in Canada, dictates to the wholesale trade not only what price their goods shall be sold at, but goes so far as to say that if other lines of syrup and canned milk made by other manufacturers are not sold at prices dictated by them, they will not supply the wholesaler with any of their goods, which is, to say the least, a highhanded proceeding. The difference in the cost of the Canadian and the American syrup delivered in Winnipeg is 58 cents per case, or 18 per cent. The freight rate is about the same, but the duty on the American syrup, tins and war tax, is 32 per cent, and still it costs 18 per cent less than the Canadian. Then there is the Crystal White syrup, which shows even a greater margin, but we will not go into the details for the present. The wholesalers' profit on canned cream is over 16 per cent, and on Edwardsburg starch nearly 18 per cent.
The E. B. Eddy Company at Ottawa fixes the price at which the jobber is to sell their goods at and distinctly states in the agreement that if any wholesale grocery house sells matches other than those made by the Eddy Company, they will refuse to supply them with their goods. Said goods carry a profit of 20 per cent to the jobber, or over double the profit that any well conducted wholesale grocery house should get.
We understand there is in this city what is called a "Grocers' Guild," composed of jobbers, who are to some extent responsible for present conditions. They are always trying to get the manufacturers to make fixed selling prices and to refuse to sell to wholesalers who do not buy exclusively from them. When they meet the manufacturer, the question usually is, not what the manufacturer is going to charge for his goods, but what margin of profit the jobber is going to get. The manufacturer left to himself no doubt takes a good profit and in many cases allows the jobber a very liberal discount, and all this is done through the combines.
I believe that every manufacturer has a right to fix his price and terms, but I do not think -he should have the right to dictate to the retailer what he shall charge, neither should any manufacturer be allowed to dictate to the jobber what he shall sell a similar line of goods for. As long as a wholesaler
[Mr. MacNutt.l
adheres to a manufacturer's selling price and terms, the manufacturer should be compelled to supply the jobber with h:s goods.
Canned goods just on the market furnishes a fair sample of the benefit of protection to the manufacturers and accounts in part at least for the high cost of living. Canadian tomatoes, 21's, -cost $3.76 per case delivered in Winnipeg; California tomatoes, 2J's, cost $3.67 per case delivered in Winnipeg, or 9 cents per case less than the Canadian, notwithstanding that the American goods paid duty of 69c per case, or equal to 30 per cent; war tax d71c, equal to 7* per cent; a difference in freight rate of 18c, or equal to 8 per cent, totalling in all 45i per cent.
Liquid veneer, another United States product, shows a margin of 97 per cent between the price paid by the jobber and the price paid by the consumer. No wonder though our friends to the south put in a small cheap plant as the duty pays for the cost in less than two years.
Of course these small plants should be protected as they are of such importance not only to Canada but to the Empire.
Clause 2 of this .amendment refers m.ore particularly to farm implements and machinery and other articles of that kind. I have only two faults to find with it. In the first place, I should like to .see wagons included. I think also that, as a matter of principle, raw material for the manufacturers affected should be provided for. I think it is only fair, when we,,are putting the products of these manufacturers on the free list, that their raw material should be placed on the free list also. While I criticise the clause in these respects, of course I support it, as it goes in the right direction and nearly as far as it is possible to
go.	-
Clause 3 says:
That staple foods and food products t other than wheat and flour), domestic animals and foods therefor, be admitted into Canada free of duty when coming from and being the product of, any country admitting like Canadian articles into such country free of duty.
I supppse that would cover barley and oats, and potatoes as well, coming from countries that admit such articles from Canada free of duty.
The Council of Agriculture, which represents not the West only but at least the province of Ontario as well, considered very carefully this question of tariff, and after full, deliberation produced a proposal somewhat similar to this amendment. They go a little further in some respect, and probably not iso far in others. These men represent the great farming interests of Ontario and the West. They are able men, men who have the interests of the country at heart. Many of them have 'been heretofore supporters of the hon. gentlemen opposite.

To-day, I do not know that that is their position; they are taking a_ thoroughly independent stand. They believe that the most important matter outside those matters relating to the war is a very considerable reduction in the tariff. But they believe also that this has a very direct connection with matters pertaining to the war. I need not enlarge upon that. We hear it from every platform, we see it in every newspaper we know it ourselves, that it is as necessary to provide shells and munitions, and to provide food, as it is to send men into the battle line. There appears to be now a very great shortage of food throughout the world. 'Crop failures have occurred in many food-producing countries. And even when food is produced, there is great difficulty in getting it to the seat of war. Still we have every faith that if the food is produced means will be found to carry it to the places where it is needed.
Now, surely it will be recognized that in this matter the farmers are not advocating merely that which is in their own selfish interests. It has a much wider significance than that. It is only common sense to say that the Government should encourage in every way the occupying of our vacant land and greater production from the soil by the people now on the land. But there is no great encouragement to men to go upon the land at the present time. Prices of farm products are high, but we know that these are war prices, that they are abnormal, and only temporary. The farmer must consider not merely the conditions during the time of war but what the conditions are to be in the future. It has been often pointed out, and is easily understood, that a great burden will rest upon the country after this war is over. Our people are perfectly willing to bear that burden, there is no doubt about that; they are ready to
sacrifice themselves in all ways, and to make every effort possible to put the full strength of the country into the winning of the war. There will be no complaint with' regard to the taxation that the country must bear after the war, so long as that taxation is the result of efficient administration and, is equitably levied. Undoubtedly the best way to meet these burdens in the future is to encourage the people to go on the land and produce. We have the land, and with great population, an increase in the production of wealth, and a condition of general prosperity throughout the country, there will be no difficulty in meeting the obligations which we are now incurring. I am satisfied the farmers will never complain, no matter what the burden may be, provided that the weight of that burden be equitably distributed.
I revert for a moment to the platform of the Council of Agriculture in order to mention one matter which seems of importance. That platform has this clause:
That the reciprocity agreement of 1911 which still remains on the United States statute book be accepted by the Parliament of Canada.
There is one point that was evidently overlooked when that clause was adopted. The reciprocity agreement only reduced the duty on agricultural implements to 15 per cent at the lowest. That fact was probably overlooked in the consideration of this matter. Of course, the whole is modified by the clauses in favour of placing a great variety of articles on the free list.

'They are comparative figures from the official returns, showing the number of acres under crop in each of the years from 1911 to 1916, and also from 1911 to 1914, showing what increases or decreases there were in normal years, and also the sudden jump in Saskatchewan and Al'berta in 1915, though the farms were operated by a less number of farmers. My argument is that these men had risen to the occasion, but that in previous years, there was a comparatively small increase in acreage. We know very well that there was a less number of farmers in the West in 1915, but notwithstanding that the farmers who were-there increased their area for war purposes. Are these men not worthy of being encouraged?

Calgary, Alta.,
May 23, 1917.
W. A. D. Buchanan,
House Parliament,
Ottawa.
The following wire has been forwarded today which is self explanatory. Hon. T. W. Crothers, Ottawa, Ont., having read your statement in the House, Monday, that coal strike would be settled in forty-eight hours, the Policy Committee of district eighteen, U.M.W. of A., respectfully inform you they have no information of any move of that kind, and being the only body authorized by the men on strike to negotiate a settlement, they are the only parties who can arrange the same.

Chairman Policy Committee.
The reason I am bringing this up is that an announcement was made that the strike would be settled within forty-eight hours, and the parties concerned say that they know nothing about any negotiations in that direction.
